entries.answer:
Aura Mutation goes to Anahi's graveyard, not exile (assuming Nehemiah's Leyline of the Void is actually destroyed by it and no other Leyline of the Void or similar replacement effect is on the battlefield).

Why: Leyline of the Void reads "If a card would be put into an opponent's graveyard from anywhere, exile it instead." That's a replacement effect, and it only functions while Leyline of the Void is on the battlefield. A spell is put into its owner's graveyard as the very last step of its own resolution — after all of its instructions have been carried out. So the order is:

1. Aura Mutation resolves and destroys Leyline of the Void. Destruction moves it to Nehemiah's graveyard immediately (its own controller's graveyard, so Leyline of the Void doesn't exile itself — it only replaces cards going to an *opponent's* graveyard).
2. Aura Mutation creates a 1/1 green Saproling token for each point of Leyline of the Void's mana value. Leyline of the Void costs {2}{B}{B}, mana value 4, so Anahi gets four Saprolings (last known information on the battlefield is used).
3. Only then is Aura Mutation itself put into Anahi's graveyard. By that moment Leyline of the Void is no longer on the battlefield, so its replacement effect no longer exists and Aura Mutation is simply put into the graveyard.

Exceptions worth checking: if Leyline of the Void is indestructible, regenerated, or otherwise not destroyed (or if it's already gone when Aura Mutation resolves, making Aura Mutation fizzle for lack of a legal target — a countered-on-resolution spell is put into the graveyard while Leyline of the Void is still out), then Aura Mutation is exiled instead. Likewise if Nehemiah controls a second Leyline of the Void or another effect with the same replacement, Aura Mutation is exiled.

Multiplayer note: in a game with more than two players, if any *other* opponent of Anahi also controls a Leyline of the Void, that one still applies and Aura Mutation is exiled. With exactly two players and only the one Leyline of the Void, Aura Mutation reaches Anahi's graveyard normally.
entries.answer_gold: Graveyard. Leyline of the Void is destroyed before Aura Mutation goes to the graveyard, since going to the graveyard is the last part of a spell resolving.

entries.question: Ari controls [Omnath, Locus of Creation] and [Elesh Norn, Mother of Machines]. They play [Tainted Peak]. What happens?

entries.answer:
Short answer: Omnath, Locus of Creation's landfall ability triggers twice off the single Tainted Peak (once normally, once more from Elesh Norn, Mother of Machines). The first trigger to resolve adds one mana of any color; the second trigger to resolve makes Ari gain 4 life. Nothing else happens from that land drop.

Why:

1. Playing Tainted Peak is a special action that doesn't use the stack. Tainted Peak has no "enters tapped" clause (it's the Torment-style land that just needs a Swamp to make colored mana), so nothing about it changes the landfall interaction.

2. Elesh Norn, Mother of Machines reads, in relevant part, "If a permanent entering the battlefield causes a triggered ability of a permanent you control to trigger, that ability triggers an additional time." Tainted Peak is a permanent entering the battlefield, and Omnath, Locus of Creation is a permanent Ari controls, so Omnath, Locus of Creation's landfall ability triggers an additional time. These are two separate triggered abilities on the stack (not copies); Ari puts them on the stack in any order and players may respond between resolutions.

Omnath, Locus of Creation's landfall ability checks how many times that ability has *resolved* this turn: the first resolution adds one mana of any color, the second resolution gains 4 life, the third resolution has Omnath, Locus of Creation deal 4 damage to each opponent. Since the two triggers resolve one at a time, the first is resolution #1 (mana) and the second is resolution #2 (4 life). Because the modes key off resolution count, not off which trigger it is, the order Ari stacks them doesn't matter here.

4. The mana added by the first resolution goes into Ari's mana pool and empties at the end of the current step or phase, so it's only usable during that main phase.

5. Follow-up land the same turn: with Elesh Norn, Mother of Machines still out, the next land Ari plays gives two more triggers — resolution #3 (Omnath, Locus of Creation deals 4 damage to each opponent) and resolution #4, which does nothing, since the ability only defines effects for the first, second, and third resolutions.

Multiplayer: nothing changes for this land drop. The only opponent-facing effect is the third-resolution damage, which would hit each opponent — so in a game with more than two players that later trigger deals 4 to every opponent, not just one. Also note Elesh Norn, Mother of Machines' second ability ("Permanents entering the battlefield don't cause abilities of permanents your opponents control to trigger") does nothing here, but it would shut off any opponents' landfall-style permanents when their own or anyone's permanents enter.

Timing note: I'm assuming Elesh Norn, Mother of Machines was already on the battlefield when Tainted Peak entered. If Elesh Norn, Mother of Machines were to enter *after* the land, Omnath, Locus of Creation would have triggered only once and Ari would only get the one mana of any color.
entries.answer_gold: Omnath, Locus of Creation's ability triggers twice. The first instance of the ability will cause Ari to gain 4 life and the second instance will add {R}{G}{U}{W} to their mana pool. Elesh Norn, Mother of Machines will cause the ability to trigger twice since it triggers as the result of a permanent entering the battlefield. Omnath, Locus of Creation's triggered ability has an effect depending on how many times its resolved this turn, so the second instance that resolves will have the second effect.

entries.question: Amiya controls [Fetid Gargantua] with two +1/+1 counters on it. Nico controls [Soul-Scar Mage] and casts [Scorching Lava] targeting Fetid Gargantua. After Scorching Lava resolves, can Fetid Gargantua adapt again?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude that Soul-Scar Mage turns the damage into -1/-1 counters which annihilate the +1/+1 counters via state-based actions, leaving no +1/+1 counters so adapt can be activated again.
entries.answer:
Yes — as long as Scorching Lava's damage is at least 2 and Fetid Gargantua survives, it will have no +1/+1 counters on it afterward, so its adapt ability will work again.

Why:

1. Soul-Scar Mage's last ability is a replacement effect: if a source Nico controls would deal noncombat damage to a creature, that many -1/-1 counters are put on that creature instead. Since Nico controls Scorching Lava, the damage event never happens — Fetid Gargantua simply receives that many -1/-1 counters instead of being dealt damage.

2. Once Fetid Gargantua has both +1/+1 counters and -1/-1 counters on it, state-based actions immediately remove them in pairs (the "annihilation" rule). With two +1/+1 counters already there, two -1/-1 counters from Scorching Lava cancel them exactly, leaving Fetid Gargantua with no counters at all and no damage marked on it.

3. Adapt N reads "If this creature has no +1/+1 counters on it, put N +1/+1 counters on it." That condition is checked when the adapt ability resolves. With zero +1/+1 counters remaining, adapt will put counters on Fetid Gargantua again. (You can activate adapt any time you could cast an instant, but if you activate it in response to Scorching Lava, the adapt ability resolves first, while the two +1/+1 counters are still there, and it does nothing — wait until Scorching Lava has fully resolved and the counters have annihilated.)

Assumptions and variations: I'm assuming Scorching Lava deals exactly 2 noncombat damage to Fetid Gargantua and that Fetid Gargantua's toughness is high enough that shrinking by the -1/-1 counters (before annihilation) doesn't kill it. If Scorching Lava dealt only 1 damage, only one +1/+1 counter would be annihilated, one +1/+1 counter would remain, and adapt would do nothing. If it dealt 3 or more, all +1/+1 counters would be gone plus leftover -1/-1 counters would stay on Fetid Gargantua; adapt would still work (there'd be no +1/+1 counters), and the new +1/+1 counters would then annihilate with the leftover -1/-1 counters.

Contrast: without Soul-Scar Mage, Scorching Lava would just mark damage on Fetid Gargantua, its two +1/+1 counters would remain, and adapt would do nothing.

Player count doesn't matter here — Soul-Scar Mage's replacement effect keys off "a source you control," so it applies to Nico's Scorching Lava the same way in a two-player or multiplayer game.
entries.answer_gold: Yes. If a permanent has both -1/-1 and +1/+1 counters on it, they are removed as a state-based action. Adapt checks the number of +1/+1 counters on Fetid Gargantua as it resolves, it doesn't matter if it's been activated in the past.

entries.question: Ari controls [Emeria Shepherd]. They play [Sacred Peaks], and target [Garenbrig Carver] in their graveyard. In response, Noelle activates [Alchemist's Refuge]. When that ability resolves, they casts [Blood Moon]. When Emeria Shepherd's ability resolves, where is Garenbrig Carver?
entries.reason: The candidate says the card stays in the graveyard (or can be paid for to go to the battlefield), which contradicts the reference's conclusion that Garenbrig Carver ends up in Ari's hand.
entries.answer:
**Garenbrig Carver is still in Ari's graveyard when Emeria Shepherd's ability begins resolving, and it will only leave if Ari chooses to pay {6} — in which case it goes to the battlefield. It does not go to Ari's hand.**

Why:

1. **Blood Moon** reads "Nonbasic lands are Mountains." Sacred Peaks is a nonbasic land, so once Blood Moon has resolved, Sacred Peaks is a Mountain and nothing else — a type‑changing effect that sets a land's subtype to a basic land type removes its other land types (and its other abilities) and gives it the intrinsic "{T}: Add {R}" ability. So even if Sacred Peaks had the Plains type printed on it, it doesn't have it anymore; and if it never had the Plains type, nothing changes. Either way, at the moment Emeria Shepherd's ability resolves, Sacred Peaks is not a Plains.

2. **Emeria Shepherd** reads: "Landfall — Whenever a land enters the battlefield under your control, if it's a Plains, return target card from your graveyard to your hand. Otherwise, you may pay {6}. If you do, return that card from your graveyard to the battlefield." Despite looking like an intervening-"if" clause, the "if it's a Plains" condition is checked **as the ability resolves**, not when it triggers — that's what makes the "Otherwise" clause meaningful. Since Sacred Peaks is a Mountain (not a Plains) at resolution, Ari gets the "otherwise" branch instead of the free return-to-hand.

3. Ari then chooses whether to pay {6} (six generic mana, payable with any colors or with colorless). If Ari pays, Garenbrig Carver — a permanent (creature) card, so a legal thing to put onto the battlefield — enters the battlefield under Ari's control as a 3/3 Human Warrior. If Ari declines or can't pay, Garenbrig Carver simply stays in the graveyard.

Notes on the surrounding pieces:

- **Alchemist's Refuge** ("{2}{G}{U}, {T}: You may cast spells this turn as though they had flash") lets Noelle, its controller, cast Blood Moon during Ari's turn with the trigger on the stack. That's the whole point of the sequence: Blood Moon changes Sacred Peaks' type *before* Emeria Shepherd's ability checks it.
- The target was locked in when the trigger went on the stack, and Garenbrig Carver is still in the graveyard, so the ability doesn't fizzle for lack of a legal target — Blood Moon doesn't touch the target at all, only the Plains/not-Plains check.
- **Timing assumption:** I'm assuming Blood Moon fully resolved before Emeria Shepherd's triggered ability resolved, as described. If instead Emeria Shepherd's ability had resolved first and Sacred Peaks was a Plains at that time, Garenbrig Carver would have gone to Ari's hand for free, and the later Blood Moon would be irrelevant to that trigger.
- **Player count:** none of this changes between a two-player and a multiplayer game; Emeria Shepherd's ability only involves its controller's graveyard, and Alchemist's Refuge only helps its own controller.
entries.answer_gold:
Ari's hand.

Blood Moon changes Sacred Peaks's subtypes to "Mountain", and Sacred Peaks loses all other subtypes. During the resolution of the ability, Sacred Peaks is no longer a Plains and therefore Garenbrig Carver will not return to the battlefield.

entries.question: Ainsley controls [General Ferrous Rokiric]. What happens when they cast [Illusion]?
entries.reason: The reference gives a definitive ruling that Rokiric won't trigger, while the candidate only gives a conditional answer depending on the spell's colors instead of stating the specific conclusion.
entries.answer:
Short answer: nothing special happens unless the spell Ainsley casts is multicolored. General Ferrous Rokiric reads "Protection from monocolored" and "Whenever you cast a multicolored spell, create a 4/4 red and white Golem artifact creature token." A spell only triggers General Ferrous Rokiric if it is two or more colors.

I should flag an assumption: I don't know of a Magic card whose name is exactly "Illusion" (Illusion is a creature type, and there are cards like Phantasmal Image, Krovikan Mist, and Illusion tokens). So I'll answer by the two readings that make sense:

1. If "Illusion" means an Illusion creature spell that is monocolored (blue, as almost all Illusions are) or colorless: General Ferrous Rokiric does not trigger. No Golem token is created. Additionally, because of protection from monocolored, a monocolored Illusion spell or ability can't target General Ferrous Rokiric, can't deal damage to it, can't enchant or equip it, and a monocolored Illusion creature can't block General Ferrous Rokiric. Protection has no effect on Ainsley's ability to cast the spell in the first place.

2. If "Illusion" is (or has been made) a multicolored spell — two or more colors from its mana cost or a color indicator: General Ferrous Rokiric's ability triggers when the spell is cast. The trigger goes on the stack above the spell and resolves first, so Ainsley gets the 4/4 red and white Golem artifact creature token before the spell resolves. The token is created even if the Illusion spell is later countered, since the trigger already happened on casting.

A few details worth knowing: the trigger checks the spell's color as it exists on the stack immediately after it's cast, so a cost-reduction or color-changing effect applied during casting can matter. "Multicolored" means two or more colors — a spell that is colorless (including one that costs {C}) is not multicolored, and neither is a single-colored spell no matter how many mana symbols of that color it has. Also note General Ferrous Rokiric is not legendary-restricted in any relevant way here, and the trigger is once per multicolored spell cast, so casting several multicolored spells makes several Golems.

Multiplayer makes no difference: General Ferrous Rokiric triggers only on spells its controller (Ainsley) casts, and protection from monocolored works identically regardless of the number of opponents.

If you can tell me the exact card you mean, I can give a precise ruling on that specific spell.
entries.answer_gold: General Ferrous Rokiric won't trigger. While Illusion is a multicolored card elsewhere, on the stack it's a monocolored card.

entries.question:
Aydan casts [Kellan, the Fae-Blooded], and Nico answers by casting [Spell Queller], exiling Kellan, the Fae-Blooded with its triggered ability.
When Spell Queller leaves the battlefield, can Aydan choose to cast [Birthright Boon] or do they have to cast Kellan, the Fae-Blooded?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion that Spell Queller’s leave-the-battlefield permission allows the owner to cast either face of the MDFC (Kellan or Birthright Boon) without paying its mana cost.
entries.answer:
Aydan may cast either face — Birthright Boon is a legal choice, and it's cast without paying its mana cost.

Why: Kellan, the Fae-Blooded // Birthright Boon is a modal double-faced card (MDFC), not a transforming double-faced card. An MDFC has two independent faces, and the player casting it announces which face they're casting as part of putting the spell on the stack. While the card is in exile (a zone other than the stack or the battlefield), it has only its front face's characteristics — so it sits in exile as Kellan, the Fae-Blooded, and its mana value there is the front face's mana value (which is what Spell Queller's enters-the-battlefield trigger checked for 'mana value 4 or less' when it exiled the spell Aydan cast).

But Spell Queller's leave-the-battlefield ability says the exiled card's owner may cast *that card* without paying its mana cost. Permission to cast a card is permission to cast either face of an MDFC; nothing ties Aydan to the face that was originally cast. So when Spell Queller leaves the battlefield and that trigger resolves, Aydan chooses on announcement whether to cast Kellan, the Fae-Blooded or Birthright Boon, and pays no mana cost either way (additional costs and any targeting requirements of the chosen face still apply).

A few practical notes:
- The casting happens during the resolution of Spell Queller's leave-the-battlefield trigger. Because the effect instructs Aydan to cast the card, timing restrictions based on card type are ignored, so Birthright Boon can be cast then even though sorceries normally require a main phase. It's a 'may' with a now-or-never window: if Aydan declines, the card simply stays in exile.
- 'Without paying its mana cost' means Aydan can't choose to pay the cost instead, and can't apply cost reductions to it; only additional costs (if any) must be paid.
- If Birthright Boon's face were a land instead of a spell, it could not be 'cast' at all — but it is a castable spell face, so this isn't an issue here.
- Contrast: if this were a transforming double-faced card (front face only castable), Aydan would be limited to the front face. Kellan, the Fae-Blooded's card is an MDFC, so both faces are on the table.

This works identically in two-player and multiplayer games; Spell Queller's trigger grants the option only to the owner of the exiled card, Aydan, regardless of how many players are in the game.
entries.answer_gold: Aydan can choose to cast either Kellan, the Fae-Blooded or Birthright Boon when Spell Queller leaves the battlefield.

entries.question: Can Nicolas cast [Memory Lapse] targeting Aubrianna's [Underworld Charger] that is escaping from their graveyard?
entries.reason: Both state that an escaped Underworld Charger is a spell on the stack and can be targeted and countered by Memory Lapse, which then puts it on top of its owner's library.
entries.answer:
Yes. A creature spell cast for its escape cost is an ordinary spell on the stack, so Nicolas can cast Memory Lapse (an instant) targeting Aubrianna's Underworld Charger in response, and if Memory Lapse resolves, Underworld Charger is countered and put on top of Aubrianna's library instead of into her graveyard.

Details:

- Escape is a keyword that lets you cast a card from your graveyard by paying its escape cost, which for Underworld Charger includes exiling other cards from your graveyard. Once Aubrianna announces the spell, Underworld Charger leaves the graveyard and exists on the stack as a normal creature spell. Escape grants no protection from being countered and does not make the spell "can't be countered."
- Memory Lapse says to counter target spell, and it replaces where that spell would go: a countered spell normally goes to its owner's graveyard, but Memory Lapse puts it on top of its owner's library instead. So Underworld Charger ends up on top of Aubrianna's library, not back in her graveyard — meaning she can't immediately escape it again; she'll draw it next turn (or sooner) and can then cast it from hand normally.
- Costs already paid are not refunded. The cards Aubrianna exiled to pay the escape cost stay in exile, and the mana she spent is gone.
- Timing assumption: I'm assuming Nicolas casts Memory Lapse while Underworld Charger is still on the stack. If he waits until Underworld Charger has already resolved and is a creature on the battlefield, Memory Lapse can no longer be used — it can only target a spell, not a permanent, and would have no legal target.
- Player count doesn't matter here. Memory Lapse can target any spell on the stack regardless of who controls it, so the ruling is identical in a two-player game and in multiplayer.
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Escape is an alternative cost ([702.138a]), which means that once paid the escaped spell is on the stack, and can be interacted with as normal. Countering a spell means to remove that spell from the stack before it resolves. Underworld Charger is a legal target for Memory Lapse.

entries.question: Ariyah has [Guardian Naga] in their graveyard. Can they flash back Guardian Naga's Adventure with [Flashback]?
entries.reason: The candidate gives the same final ruling — you cannot flashback an Adventure from the graveyard because the Adventure characteristics (and any flashback on that half) don't exist there, matching the reference.
entries.answer:
**Short answer: no — not under the normal Adventure rules.** While Guardian Naga is sitting in Ariyah's graveyard, the card has only its "normal" (creature) characteristics. The Adventure half's name, type, mana cost, and *abilities* — including a flashback ability printed on it — simply don't exist in the graveyard, so there's no flashback permission for Ariyah to use. The only exception is if Guardian Naga's own printed text explicitly says that ability functions from the graveyard; printed card text beats the general rule.

Definitions this hinges on:
- **Adventure**: a card with an Adventure has an alternative set of characteristics (usually an instant or sorcery) that are used *only while the card is on the stack as an Adventure spell*. In every other zone — hand, graveyard, exile, battlefield — the card is just the creature card (e.g., in the graveyard it is a creature card named Guardian Naga, not a sorcery).
- **Flashback**: a keyword on instants and sorceries meaning "You may cast this card from your graveyard by paying its flashback cost rather than its mana cost," plus "exile it instead of putting it anywhere else when it leaves the stack." It's an ability of the card that must *function in the graveyard* to grant that permission — which is exactly what the Adventure rules prevent for an Adventure-half ability.

A useful comparison: Bonecrusher Giant's Stomp half doesn't exist anywhere except on the stack; in the graveyard the card is only Bonecrusher Giant. The same logic applies to Guardian Naga.

What *would* let Ariyah cast Guardian Naga's Adventure from the graveyard: a separate effect that grants permission to cast the card from the graveyard (Yawgmoth's Will–style "you may play cards from your graveyard this turn"). When you have permission to cast the card, you may choose to cast it as its Adventure. Note that permissions worded as "cast an instant or sorcery card from your graveyard" (Underworld Breach, for example) do **not** work, because in the graveyard Guardian Naga is a creature card, not an instant or sorcery card.

A caveat on the card itself: I don't have reliable knowledge of a card named Guardian Naga whose Adventure has flashback. If it really is printed that way, then by design its text must be doing something the general rule doesn't (or it's from a rules update I can't confirm), and you should follow the printed text — read it carefully for wording like "this ability functions from your graveyard" or flashback printed on the creature half. If instead the flashback is on the *creature* half, that would be nonfunctional as written for casting the creature (flashback is for instants and sorceries) and you'd again need the card's own text to explain it.

Secondary note (only if some effect does let it happen): if an Adventure spell resolves it's exiled "on an adventure," and the owner may later cast the creature from exile; flashback's own exile replacement would also send it to exile. Which permission you end up with there is an edge case I wouldn't assume without the actual card text.

Player count doesn't matter here — the answer is the same in a two-player game or a multiplayer game.
entries.answer_gold: No. An Adventure defines alternative characteristics the card can have when cast as an Adventure. Adventurer cards only have their normal characteristics in every zone other than the stack, so it's not a legal target for Flashback.

entries.question: Ace controls [Sarkhan, the Dragonspeaker] and activates its ability, turning it into a creature. They then play a second Sarkhan, the Dragonspeaker. What happens when the second Sarkhan, the Dragonspeaker resolves?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude the legend rule applies and Ace must choose one Sarkhan, putting the other into their graveyard because both are legendary permanents with the same name.
entries.answer:
The legend rule applies: as soon as the second Sarkhan, the Dragonspeaker resolves and enters the battlefield, Ace controls two legendary permanents named Sarkhan, the Dragonspeaker, so the next time state-based actions are checked Ace chooses one to keep and the other is put into its owner's graveyard.

Why the animated one doesn't dodge the legend rule:

- Sarkhan, the Dragonspeaker's +1 ability reads "Until end of turn, Sarkhan, the Dragonspeaker becomes a legendary 4/4 red Dragon creature with flying. Prevent all damage that would be dealt to him this turn." Because the ability doesn't say "he's still a planeswalker," the new card type (creature) replaces the planeswalker type for the rest of the turn — but note the ability explicitly re-grants the legendary supertype, and it still has the same name.
- The legend rule keys off name plus the legendary supertype, not card type. It doesn't matter that one Sarkhan, the Dragonspeaker is currently a Dragon creature and the other is a planeswalker; they're both legendary permanents named Sarkhan, the Dragonspeaker controlled by Ace, so one must go.
- (Historically, before the 2017 rules change, planeswalkers used a separate "planeswalker uniqueness rule" based on subtype, and an animated Sarkhan, the Dragonspeaker arguably could have coexisted with a freshly cast one. That rule no longer exists — everything now runs through the legend rule.)

Whichever one Ace keeps:

- Keep the animated one: the newly cast Sarkhan, the Dragonspeaker card goes to Ace's graveyard from the battlefield (it did resolve and enter the battlefield first, so any enters-the-battlefield triggers or "enters with loyalty counters" happen, and it's not countered). The survivor remains a 4/4 flying Dragon with damage prevented for the turn, keeps its loyalty counters (5 if it started at 4 and used +1), and reverts to being just a planeswalker as the turn ends.
- Keep the new one: the animated 4/4 Dragon goes to the graveyard, and Ace has a fresh Sarkhan, the Dragonspeaker planeswalker at its starting loyalty of 4 — and it can activate a loyalty ability this turn, since loyalty-ability usage is tracked per permanent, and this is a new object.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming the +1 was activated and resolved before the second Sarkhan, the Dragonspeaker was cast, as stated. If instead the second copy resolved first, the legend rule would fire at that moment anyway — the outcome is the same, just without a Dragon on board to choose between.

Player count doesn't matter: the legend rule only looks at permanents a single player controls, so the answer is identical in two-player and multiplayer games. Opponents controlling their own Sarkhan, the Dragonspeaker is irrelevant.
entries.answer_gold: As soon as the spell finishes resolving, state-based actions are checked and Ace will need to choose one Sarkhan, the Dragonspeaker to put into their graveyard. Regardless of what card type they are, both Sarkhan, the Dragonspeaker are legendary permanents with the same name, and therefore the 'legend rule' applies.

entries.question: Ainsley controls [Reconnaissance] and attacks Nancy with [Loxodon Wayfarer]. After combat damage is dealt, can Ainsley use Reconnaissance's activated ability to untap Loxodon Wayfarer?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude that Loxodon Wayfarer is still an attacking creature in the combat damage step/through end of combat and so is a legal target for Reconnaissance, allowing it to be removed from combat and untapped.
entries.answer:
Yes — as long as Ainsley activates it while Loxodon Wayfarer is still an attacking creature, which it remains for the rest of the combat damage step and through the end of combat step.

How it works:

- Reconnaissance reads "{0}: Remove target attacking creature you control from combat. Untap that creature." It has no timing restriction beyond the normal rule that an activated ability can be activated whenever its controller has priority. Ainsley gets priority right after combat damage is dealt (still in the combat damage step), so Ainsley can pay {0}, target Loxodon Wayfarer, and resolve the ability there.
- "Removed from combat" means Loxodon Wayfarer stops being an attacking creature; it's no longer attacking Nancy. This does nothing to undo damage that has already been dealt — Nancy has already been dealt the combat damage, and any "deals combat damage" triggers have already triggered and won't be countered by the removal.
- The untap is a separate, immediate effect of the same ability, so Loxodon Wayfarer ends up untapped and out of combat. That's the classic Reconnaissance use: swing, connect, then untap so the creature is available to block on an opponent's turn or to be tapped for a cost.
- Caveat about Loxodon Wayfarer specifically: if Loxodon Wayfarer didn't tap to attack (e.g., it has vigilance or was already untapped), the untap portion simply does nothing and only the removal from combat matters. And if Loxodon Wayfarer has already been dealt lethal damage by blockers, untapping it doesn't save it — it's still destroyed by state-based actions, since removing a creature from combat doesn't remove damage marked on it.

Timing assumption: I'm reading "after combat damage is dealt" as the priority window in the combat damage step following damage. If instead Ainsley waits until the end of combat step, the activation still works, because creatures don't stop being attacking creatures until that step ends. If Ainsley waits until the combat phase is over (postcombat main phase), Reconnaissance has no legal target and the ability can't be activated at all.

Multiplayer note: nothing changes with more than two players. Removing Loxodon Wayfarer from combat only affects its own attack on Nancy; other players' creatures and other attackers remain in combat normally, and Loxodon Wayfarer being untapped afterward lets it block during any other player's turn.
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Loxodon Wayfarer is considered an attacking creature until the end of the combat phase, and is therefore still a legal target for Reconnaissance's activated ability.

entries.question: Arjun controls [Thermopod] and has no cards in their graveyard. Assuming they have enough mana, can they activate [Molten-Tail Masticore]'s first activated ability?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same bottom-line ruling as the reference: the activated ability can be put on the stack with an empty graveyard, then you may activate Thermopod to sacrifice a creature (including the Masticore) to the graveyard and exile it to pay the ability's cost.
entries.answer:
Yes. Arjun can activate Molten-Tail Masticore's ability ({2}, Exile a creature card from your graveyard: Molten-Tail Masticore deals 4 damage to any target) even starting with an empty graveyard, because during the activation process Arjun can sacrifice a creature *card* to Thermopod's mana ability ("Sacrifice a creature: Add {R}"), putting that card into the graveyard in time to be exiled as the ability's cost.

Why this works — the activation steps (rule 602.2b applies the spell-casting steps to activated abilities):
1. Announce the ability and put it on the stack.
2. Choose the target for the 4 damage (any target).
3. Determine the total cost: {2} plus "exile a creature card from your graveyard." Note the {2} is generic, so Thermopod's red mana can pay part or all of it.
4. Activate mana abilities (601.2g). Here Arjun sacrifices a creature to Thermopod. Because that creature is a card, it goes to the graveyard immediately (this is a cost of the mana ability, paid on activation — mana abilities don't use the stack).
5. Pay the total cost (601.2h). Only now does Arjun choose which creature card in the graveyard to exile — and the creature just sacrificed to Thermopod is sitting there.

Important restrictions:
- The sacrificed creature must be a creature *card*, not a token. A token that dies ceases to exist as a state-based action and never provides a card to exile.
- Arjun may sacrifice Thermopod itself to its own ability; Thermopod is a creature card, so it lands in the graveyard and can then be exiled to pay Molten-Tail Masticore's cost.
- Arjun may even sacrifice Molten-Tail Masticore itself; its ability is already on the stack and resolves independently of the source (though it would then be in the graveyard and could be the card exiled).
- The ability still needs {2} total; Thermopod's {R} counts toward that generic portion, and Arjun must have the rest available.

Contrast with delve/convoke-style keywords: those must be applied when the total cost is *determined* (before mana abilities are activated), so the same trick wouldn't fuel delve. Molten-Tail Masticore's exile is an ordinary cost paid in the payment step, which is why it works.

This answer doesn't change between a two-player and a multiplayer game; the only multiplayer wrinkle is that "any target" may be a creature, planeswalker, battle, or any player/opponent at the table, chosen when the ability is put on the stack.
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Arjun first puts the ability onto the stack, after which it won't matter if Molten-Tail Masticore is on the battlefield anymore. Arjun then has a chance to activate mana abilities, at which point they can sacrifice Molten-Tail Masticore. Then Arjun pays the cost of the spell, exiling Molten-Tail Masticore from their graveyard.

entries.question: Can Ashley pay {B}{B}{B}{B}{B}{B} to cast [Beseech the Queen] or is Ashley limited to only paying {B}{B}{B} to do so?
entries.reason: Both conclude Ashley may choose for each {2/B} to pay 2 generic or B and therefore may cast Beseech the Queen for {6} (including using six black mana) rather than being limited to only {B}{B}{B}.
entries.answer:
Yes — Ashley can pay {B}{B}{B}{B}{B}{B} to cast Beseech the Queen if Ashley wants to. Ashley is not limited to {B}{B}{B}.

Why: Beseech the Queen's mana cost is {2/B}{2/B}{2/B}. {2/B} is a monocolored hybrid symbol, and each one may be paid with either two generic mana or one black mana. Ashley chooses independently for each of the three symbols while casting Beseech the Queen (as part of determining the total cost during the casting process, before mana is actually paid).

That gives Ashley these legal payment options for Beseech the Queen:
- All three symbols as {B}: three black mana total ({B}{B}{B}).
- All three as generic: {6}, which can be paid with any six mana — including six black mana, since generic mana can be paid with mana of any type, colored or colorless.
- Any mix, e.g. {B}{B} plus {2} (two black + two other mana), etc.

So "paying {B}{B}{B}{B}{B}{B}" is really "paying {6} using black mana for all of it," which is perfectly legal. It's normally wasteful, but it can matter if some other effect cares about how much mana was spent or that black mana was spent (for example, an effect that requires spending {B} on a spell, or a card that triggers on mana spent), or if an effect like Trinisphere/Thalia-style tax has already raised the cost.

One thing that does not change: the mana value of Beseech the Queen is always 6, because each {2/B} counts as 2 toward mana value, no matter which way Ashley pays. Beseech the Queen's own reminder text says this explicitly.

This is the same in a two-player game and in multiplayer; nothing about the payment choice depends on the number of opponents.
entries.answer_gold: After the first step of casting a spell, which is announcing it and moving it to the stack, Ashley makes choices regarding modes, alternative costs, additional costs, etc. This step includes deciding whether they will be paying {B} or {2} for each hybrid symbol ({2/B}) in Beseech the Queen's mana cost. They may always choose to cast it for {6} instead of {B}{B}{B} (or {2}{B}{B} or {4}{B}). Later on during the casting of the spell, the colorless parts of the mana cost may be paid with any color, including black.

entries.question: Arielle has [Blessed Hippogriff] in their graveyard. Arielle casts [Mission Briefing], can they choose to cast the adventure of Blessed Hippogriff?
entries.reason: Both the candidate and the reference conclude Mission Briefing can't target the Adventure because in the graveyard Blessed Hippogriff is a creature card, not an instant or sorcery.
entries.answer:
No. Blessed Hippogriff can't be chosen by Mission Briefing at all, so Arielle can't use Mission Briefing to cast its Adventure half.

Why: Mission Briefing ({U}{U} sorcery) reads "Surveil 2, then you may cast target instant or sorcery card from your graveyard this turn. If that card would be put into your graveyard this turn, exile it instead." The target must be an instant or sorcery *card*, and legality is checked based on the card's characteristics in the graveyard.

An Adventurer card like Blessed Hippogriff only uses its Adventure characteristics (name, mana cost, type line, and text of the Adventure half) while it's on the stack having been cast as an Adventure, and while it's exiled "on an adventure." In every other zone — including the graveyard — Blessed Hippogriff is simply a creature card with the mana cost and type line of its creature half. So in Arielle's graveyard, Blessed Hippogriff is a creature card, not an instant card, and it is not a legal target for Mission Briefing.

Two practical consequences:

1. Mission Briefing requires a legal target to be cast at all. If Blessed Hippogriff is the only relevant card in Arielle's graveyard, Arielle can't legally cast Mission Briefing — there'd be no legal target.
2. The target for Mission Briefing is chosen when Mission Briefing is cast, before the surveil 2 happens. So a card milled into the graveyard by that surveil can never be the card Mission Briefing lets you cast, and surveilling Blessed Hippogriff into the graveyard doesn't help either way.

This is the same reason Snapcaster Mage, Torrential Gearhulk, and similar "instant or sorcery card in a graveyard" effects can't interact with Adventure halves of cards sitting in a graveyard. Nothing changes based on player count — this is purely a characteristics-in-zones question, so the answer is identical in two-player and multiplayer games.

If Arielle wants to cast the Adventure (Tyr's Blessing) from the graveyard, they'd need an effect that lets them cast a *creature card* (or "a card") from their graveyard, since the permission to cast the card is what matters — an effect allowing Blessed Hippogriff to be cast from the graveyard generally allows casting it as its Adventure, provided the effect doesn't restrict it to casting it as a creature spell.
entries.answer_gold: No. Adventurer cards have an alternative set of characteristics, however any time an Adventurer card is anywhere other than the stack it only has the characteristics of the creature portion. Mission Briefing requires Arielle to choose an instant or sorcery card in their graveyard, and they cannot choose Blessed Hippogriff.

entries.question: Neriah controls [Cliffhaven Sell-Sword]. Ari casts [Oubliette] targeting it. Will Cliffhaven Sell-Sword phase back in at the beginning of Neriah's next untap step?
entries.reason: The candidate gives the same ruling as the reference: Oubliette causes the creature to phase out until Oubliette leaves, preventing the normal untap-step phasing-in.
entries.answer:
**No.** Cliffhaven Sell-Sword stays phased out for as long as Oubliette remains on the battlefield. It phases back in only when Oubliette leaves the battlefield, not at the beginning of Neriah's next untap step.

**Why:**

- Oubliette's current Oracle text is an enchantment with the triggered ability "When Oubliette enters the battlefield, target creature phases out until Oubliette leaves the battlefield." (Note that the Oubliette *spell* doesn't target; the enters-the-battlefield trigger is what targets Cliffhaven Sell-Sword. Neriah can respond to that trigger.)
- *Phasing out* means the permanent is treated as though it doesn't exist: it can't be attacked, blocked, targeted, or affected by anything, and its static abilities stop applying. It doesn't change zones — Cliffhaven Sell-Sword is still on the battlefield, still owned and controlled by Neriah, still with its counters and any attached Auras/Equipment (those phase out indirectly along with it). No leaves-the-battlefield or dies triggers occur.
- Normally a phased-out permanent phases in during its controller's untap step, before untapping. But a "phases out until [event]" effect overrides that default: the permanent skips its controller's untap steps entirely and phases in the moment the stated event happens. Here that event is Oubliette leaving the battlefield (destroyed, bounced, exiled, sacrificed, etc.).
- When Oubliette does leave, Cliffhaven Sell-Sword phases in immediately under Neriah's control, tapped or untapped exactly as it was, with the same counters and attachments. Phasing in is not "entering the battlefield," so Cliffhaven Sell-Sword's enters-the-battlefield/kicker trigger does not trigger again, and summoning sickness rules apply normally based on how long Neriah has continuously controlled it (control never lapsed, so if it was already under Neriah's control since their last turn began, it can attack/tap right away).

**Timing caveat:** if Oubliette were somehow removed in response to its own enters-the-battlefield trigger (before the trigger resolves), the trigger simply does nothing — Cliffhaven Sell-Sword never phases out at all, so there's nothing to phase back in.

**Multiplayer:** the answer is the same with any number of players. The duration is tied to Oubliette leaving the battlefield, not to turn order, and Cliffhaven Sell-Sword returns under Neriah's control regardless of whose turn it is when Oubliette leaves.
entries.answer_gold: No. Effects that phase a permanent out until a certain event prevent that permanent from phasing back in normally.

entries.question: Nico controls [Lazav, the Multifarious], which is currently a copy of [Lazav, Dimir Mastermind]. Abram discards [Kasimir the Lone Wolf] due to hand size at the end of their turn. Lazav, the Multifarious's ability triggers. After it resolves, what is Lazav, the Multifarious named?
entries.reason: Both state that if the trigger is accepted Lazav becomes named "Lazav, Dimir Mastermind" (the candidate reaches the same final naming conclusion as the reference).
entries.answer:
After the trigger resolves (assuming Nico accepts the optional "you may"), the permanent is named **Lazav, Dimir Mastermind**.

Why: Lazav, the Multifarious is currently under a copy effect making it a copy of Lazav, Dimir Mastermind, except that its name is Lazav, the Multifarious, it's legendary, and it has Lazav, the Multifarious's own {X} activated ability. Because it's a copy of Lazav, Dimir Mastermind, it has that card's triggered ability: "Whenever a creature card is put into an opponent's graveyard from anywhere, you may have Lazav, Dimir Mastermind become a copy of that card, except its name is Lazav, Dimir Mastermind, it's legendary in addition to its other types, and it has this ability."

Kasimir the Lone Wolf is a creature card and was put into an opponent's graveyard from Abram's hand, so that ability triggers. When it resolves and Nico chooses to apply it, a new copy effect is created: the permanent becomes a copy of Kasimir the Lone Wolf, **except** its name is Lazav, Dimir Mastermind, it's legendary in addition to its other types, and it has that same triggered ability. Copy effects all apply in layer 1 in timestamp order, and this newer copy effect completely replaces what the object was copying before. So the name exception from the new effect (Lazav, Dimir Mastermind) overwrites the old name exception (Lazav, the Multifarious).

Resulting board state for that permanent:
- Name: Lazav, Dimir Mastermind
- Everything else copied from Kasimir the Lone Wolf (mana cost, colors, power/toughness, subtypes, its printed abilities), plus the supertype legendary
- It has Lazav, Dimir Mastermind's triggered ability (so it can keep doing this)
- It **no longer** has Lazav, the Multifarious's "{X}: become a copy of target creature card in your graveyard" ability, since the new copy effect's exceptions don't grant that ability

Timing note: discarding down to hand size happens during the cleanup step. A triggered ability that triggers then goes on the stack and players receive priority during that cleanup step, and once everything resolves, another cleanup step happens.

Two other points: (1) The ability is optional. If Nico declines, nothing changes and the permanent stays a copy of Lazav, Dimir Mastermind named Lazav, the Multifarious. (2) Multiplayer doesn't change anything here — the trigger only cares that the creature card went to *an* opponent's graveyard, so it works the same with two players or more; it simply wouldn't trigger for a teammate's discard in a Two-Headed Giant-style game.
entries.answer_gold: "Lazav, Dimir Mastermind". Lazav, Dimir Mastermind's ability changes the card's name to "Lazav, Dimir Mastermind", regardless of what it was originally named.

entries.question: Alivia has [Road // Ruin] in their graveyard. Alivia casts [Torrential Gearhulk]. Which side of Road // Ruin can Alivia cast with its trigger?
entries.reason: The reference says Alivia may cast either half of Road // Ruin, while the candidate restricts casting to only the half that is an instant, giving a different bottom-line ruling.
entries.answer:
**Direct answer: only the half of Road // Ruin that is itself an instant.** Torrential Gearhulk's trigger reads "you may cast target instant card from your graveyard without paying its mana cost," and that permission is limited to casting an instant — Alivia can't use it to cast a sorcery half (and can never "cast" a land half at all, since lands are played, not cast).

Why the card is even a legal target: in every zone other than the stack, a split card has the **combined** characteristics of its two halves. So a split card in the graveyard with one instant half and one sorcery half is simultaneously an instant card and a sorcery card, which makes it a legal target for Torrential Gearhulk's triggered ability. The choice of which half to cast is made only when Alivia actually begins casting it, as the card is put onto the stack — and at that point the half chosen has to match the permission Torrential Gearhulk granted. (This is the same reason cascade into a modal double-faced card doesn't let you cast a back face that fails the restriction.)

So, applied to Road // Ruin:
- If exactly one half is an instant, that is the only half Alivia may cast.
- If both halves are instants, Alivia freely picks either one.
- If neither half is an instant (e.g., both sorceries), the card isn't an instant card at all and Torrential Gearhulk's ability can't even target it.
- If one half is a land face, that face can never be cast, so only the spell half is available (and only if it's an instant).

I can't verify from memory the exact printed type line of each half of Road // Ruin, so match it to the case above; the rules principle is what governs.

Two extra points: Alivia casts the spell during the resolution of Torrential Gearhulk's triggered ability, so timing restrictions (like "cast only as a sorcery") are ignored for *when* it's cast — but that never converts the permission into permission to cast a non-instant half. And because of Torrential Gearhulk's replacement effect, if that spell would be put into Alivia's graveyard this turn (on resolution, or if it's countered), it's exiled instead.

Player count doesn't change anything here: Torrential Gearhulk's ability only looks at Alivia's own graveyard, so the answer is identical in a two-player game and in multiplayer.
entries.answer_gold: Either side. Torrential Gearhulk has a targeting restriction that requires Alivia to select an instant in their graveyard. Split cards have the type of both sides simultaneously. Therefore Road // Ruin is both an instant and a sorcery card and satisfies the targeting restriction on Torrential Gearhulk. When Alivia goes to cast Road // Ruin, nothing cares about which half is cast, so either is legal.

entries.question: Alvaro controls [Draugr Thought-Thief] and [Lotusguard Disciple]. Nico controls [Sands of Time] and [Yurlok of Scorch Thrash]. If Alvaro casts [Zagras, Thief of Heartbeats], can they choose to only have the cost reduced by {1}?
entries.reason: Both conclude "No" — the spell's applicable cost reductions are applied automatically and in full, not optionally, so Alvaro can't choose to only take a {1} reduction.
entries.answer:
No. Cost reductions are not optional, and you never get to pick how much of one to apply. Alvaro must apply Zagras, Thief of Heartbeats's full reduction — {1} for each creature that died this turn — even if he'd rather pay more.

Why: when you cast a spell, you determine its total cost during casting (CR 601.2f). You start with the mana cost, add any applicable cost increases, then apply all applicable cost reductions; every effect that applies is applied automatically. Zagras, Thief of Heartbeats says "This spell costs {1} less to cast for each creature that died this turn," which is a fixed, mandatory amount — not a "you may" choice like Convoke or Improvise (where you choose how many creatures to tap). Once the total cost is locked in, Alvaro pays exactly that amount, no more and no less (CR 601.2h).

Two related points on the numbers:
- Only the generic portion of Zagras, Thief of Heartbeats's cost shrinks. The colored symbols ({B} and {R}) are untouched no matter how many creatures died, and the generic part can't go below {0}. So with, say, three creatures dead this turn, Alvaro pays the printed cost minus {3} of generic, still plus {B}{R}.
- If Alvaro produces extra mana anyway, it simply sits in his mana pool; he can't shove it into Zagras, Thief of Heartbeats.

The other permanents don't change this:
- Sands of Time (Nico's) only messes with untapping/tapping during untap steps and upkeeps. It has no effect on how a spell's cost is calculated.
- Yurlok of Scorch Thrash (Nico's) stops unspent mana from emptying as steps and phases end (overriding the normal rule that mana pools empty, CR 500.4) and makes players lose life for mana left unspent. That's a reason Alvaro shouldn't float extra mana — but it still doesn't let him volunteer to pay more for Zagras, Thief of Heartbeats.
- Draugr Thought-Thief and Lotusguard Disciple are Alvaro's own creatures; unless one of them literally reads that it changes what a spell costs, they're irrelevant to the total cost of Zagras, Thief of Heartbeats. If one of them does carry a cost-altering ability, that ability would likewise be applied automatically and in full, not at Alvaro's option (and if such a card's text explicitly says the controller "may" apply it, the card's wording wins and that one is optional).

This is the same with two players or more than two: cost determination is a purely mechanical, per-caster calculation. The only multiplayer wrinkle is that Yurlok of Scorch Thrash's mana retention and life loss apply to every player at the table, not just Alvaro and Nico.
entries.answer_gold: No. Zagras, Thief of Heartbeats's cost is reduced by the number of creatures in Alvaro's party, which is determined by the game, and is calculated to be the highest possible amount.

entries.question: Adriel controls [Oko, Thief of Crowns], [Gilded Goose], and a Food token. Adriel uses Oko, Thief of Crowns's +1 ability to make the Food token into a 3/3 Elk. Can Adriel then sacrifice it to Gilded Goose?
entries.reason: Both the candidate and reference state that Oko's +1 removes the Food artifact type (and its abilities), so the Elk token is no longer a Food and cannot be sacrificed to Gilded Goose.
entries.answer:
No. Once Oko, Thief of Crowns's +1 ability resolves on the Food token, that token is no longer a Food, so it can't be sacrificed to pay the cost of Gilded Goose's "{T}, Sacrifice a Food: Add one mana of any color" ability.

Why:

- Oko, Thief of Crowns's +1 reads "Target artifact or creature loses all abilities and becomes a green Elk creature with base power and toughness 3/3." Because it says the permanent "becomes a green Elk creature" (and not "in addition to its other types"), the new card type replaces the old one: the token stops being an artifact and becomes only a creature. When the artifact card type goes away, its artifact subtypes go away with it — and Food is an artifact subtype, not a creature type. The token's only creature type becomes Elk. (Gatherer's ruling on Oko, Thief of Crowns states plainly that the affected permanent loses its other card types and creature types.)
- Separately, "loses all abilities" strips the token's own "{2}, {T}, Sacrifice this artifact: You gain 3 life" ability, so you can't use the Food's life-gain ability either.
- Gilded Goose's mana ability requires sacrificing a Food specifically. A 3/3 green Elk creature token doesn't qualify, so the cost can't be paid with it. It could still be sacrificed to any effect that just asks for "a creature" or "a permanent."

Layer note (why this sticks): the type change happens in layer 4 (type-changing effects) and the ability removal in layer 6 (ability-adding/removing effects); both come from the same continuous effect and last indefinitely, so nothing later in the turn restores Food-ness on its own.

Adriel can still get a Food to feed Gilded Goose by activating Gilded Goose's other ability, {4}{G}, {T}: Create a Food token (note the {G} is a green mana specifically and the {4} is generic), or by using Oko, Thief of Crowns's +2 ability, which creates a Food token, on a later turn. Also worth noting: the Elk token isn't a creature Adriel just gained control of only in the sense of summoning sickness mattering — sacrificing doesn't require tapping, so summoning sickness wouldn't have been an obstacle anyway.

Nothing here changes between a two-player and a multiplayer game.
entries.answer_gold: No. Oko, Thief of Crowns's ability is a type-changing effect which will overwrite any previous types and subtypes the object had. When Gilded Goose asks Adriel to sacrifice a Food, it is saying that Adriel needs to sacrifice a permanent with the subtype "Food".

entries.question: Natasha controls a [Lifeline] and 2 [Scarwood Goblins]. Adriel casts [Plague Wind]. Does Lifeline trigger and return the creatures to the battlefield at the beginning of the next end step?
entries.reason: The candidate says the Goblins can return if any creature remains after Plague Wind, whereas the reference concludes they do not return in the given scenario because Lifeline’s intervening "if" fails when no other creature is on the battlefield.
entries.answer:
**Yes — as long as at least one creature is still on the battlefield after Plague Wind finishes resolving.** Plague Wind destroys all creatures its controller (Adriel) doesn't control, so Adriel's own creatures survive. If Adriel has even one creature left (or any other player's creature survives), Lifeline triggers separately for each Scarwood Goblins that died, and at the beginning of the next end step each Scarwood Goblins is returned to the battlefield under its owner's control.

Details and the important caveats:

- **Lifeline itself survives.** Lifeline is an enchantment, not a creature, so Plague Wind doesn't touch it — but Lifeline also doesn't count as "another creature" for its own ability.
- **"Can't be regenerated" is irrelevant.** Lifeline doesn't regenerate anything; it returns the card from the graveyard to the battlefield as a brand-new object (untapped, no damage, no prior counters or auras).
- **The two Scarwood Goblins don't count each other.** Both are destroyed simultaneously by Plague Wind, so at the moment Lifeline's ability would trigger neither Scarwood Goblins is on the battlefield to satisfy the "another creature is on the battlefield" condition for the other. The surviving creature has to be someone else's — in practice, one of Adriel's creatures. If Adriel controlled no creatures and no other player had a creature survive, Lifeline would not trigger at all and both Scarwood Goblins would stay in the graveyard.
- **The condition is checked twice.** "If another creature is on the battlefield" is an intervening-"if" clause: it must be true when the ability would trigger and again when that triggered ability resolves. Once it resolves, it sets up a delayed triggered ability that returns the card at the beginning of the next end step; the condition is not re-checked at that point. (If a Scarwood Goblins card leaves the graveyard before then, it obviously can't return.)
- **Owner, not controller.** Each Scarwood Goblins returns under its *owner's* control. If Natasha owns them, she gets them back; if she was controlling cards owned by someone else, that player gets them.
- **Lifeline is symmetrical.** It triggers for every creature that dies, not just Natasha's. So in a game with more than two players, every other player's creatures destroyed by Plague Wind would also come back at the beginning of the next end step (under their owners' control), which makes Plague Wind mostly a temporary sweeper while Lifeline is out. In a strict two-player game, the only creatures dying are Natasha's, and the survivors that enable the triggers must be Adriel's.
- **Timing assumption:** I'm assuming Plague Wind resolves and the deaths all happen at once during its resolution, with nothing else killing Adriel's remaining creatures in the meantime. If, in response to Lifeline's triggers, someone removes the last surviving creature before those triggers resolve, the intervening-"if" check fails on resolution and the Scarwood Goblins stay dead.
entries.answer_gold: No. Leaves-the-battlefield triggers care about the game state immediately before the event in question occurred when determining whether they trigger. There was another creature on the battlefield at that time, so Lifeline will trigger for both creatures that died. However, Lifeline has an intervening "if" clause that checks for that condition again as the trigger begins to resolve. There is not another creature on the battlefield at that time, so the ability is removed from the stack. Neither Scarwood Goblins returns to the battlefield.

entries.question: Alfred casts [Stream of Thought], replicating it twice. Nico controls [Chalice of the Void] with 1 charge counter. What happens?
entries.reason: The candidate says Chalice never triggers and all three instances resolve, but the reference states Chalice triggers and counters the original spell while the two replicate-created copies still resolve.
entries.answer:
Nothing happens from Chalice of the Void — it never triggers, and all three instances of Stream of Thought (the original plus both replicate copies) resolve normally.

Why:

1. Chalice of the Void reads "Whenever a player casts a spell with mana value equal to the number of charge counters on Chalice of the Void, counter that spell." With 1 charge counter, it only triggers on spells with mana value 1. Stream of Thought's mana cost is {3}{U}, so its mana value is 4. No trigger.

2. Replicate ({1}{U} on Stream of Thought) is an additional cost you choose to pay any number of times as you cast the spell, plus a triggered ability that triggers on casting and creates that many copies of the spell on the stack. Alfred replicating twice pays {3}{U} + {1}{U} + {1}{U} = {5}{U}{U}{U} total (five generic, three blue).

3. The replicate copies are *created on the stack*, not cast. Chalice of the Void only cares about spells being cast, so even if the numbers lined up, the copies would never trigger it. (Incidentally, a copy of Stream of Thought also has mana value 4, copied from the original's mana cost — the {1}{U} replicate cost paid does not become the copy's mana value.)

How it resolves: the replicate trigger goes on the stack above Stream of Thought, so it resolves first, putting the two copies on the stack. Alfred may choose new targets for each copy. The two copies resolve first, then the original Stream of Thought. Each instance does: target player mills four cards, then shuffle up to four target cards from a single graveyard into their owner's library.

Note for contrast: if Nico's Chalice of the Void had 4 charge counters, it would trigger on Alfred casting Stream of Thought and counter it — but the replicate trigger already triggered on casting, so the two copies would still be created and would still resolve. Countering the original spell doesn't stop the copies.

This is the same in a two-player game or a multiplayer game; nothing here depends on the number of players, other than Alfred choosing which player each instance of Stream of Thought mills.
entries.answer_gold: The original Stream of Thought is countered, the two copies resolve as normal. Replicate and Chalice of the Void both trigger when the spell is cast. Since the Chalice of the Void trigger is controlled by the player last in turn order, it will resolve first, countering Stream of Thought. Then Stream of Thought's trigger resolves and creates two copies of Stream of Thought. The copies are not cast, so they don't trigger Chalice of the Void.

entries.question: Adrienne attacks with [Sporeweb Weaver], and Nicolas blocks it with [Serpent Assassin]. Can Nicolas use [Tishana's Tidebinder] to counter Sporeweb Weaver's ability?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same final ruling—that Tishana's Tidebinder can target and counter Sporeweb Weaver's triggered ability on the stack (hexproof on the creature doesn't prevent targeting the ability).
entries.answer:
Yes. Once Sporeweb Weaver is dealt combat damage by Serpent Assassin, Sporeweb Weaver's "Whenever Sporeweb Weaver is dealt damage, create a 1/1 green Saproling creature token" ability triggers and goes on the stack. Because Tishana's Tidebinder has flash, Nicolas can cast it right then, in the combat damage step, while that trigger is still on the stack. Tishana's Tidebinder resolves, its enter-the-battlefield trigger goes on the stack above Sporeweb Weaver's trigger and targets it, and on resolution Sporeweb Weaver's trigger is countered — no Saproling token is created. In addition, because an ability of a permanent was countered this way, Sporeweb Weaver loses all abilities (its reach and deathtouch, and its damage trigger) for as long as Tishana's Tidebinder remains on the battlefield, so later damage to Sporeweb Weaver won't trigger it again.

A few details that matter:

1. Timing/order assumed: combat damage is dealt by Sporeweb Weaver and Serpent Assassin simultaneously in the combat damage step, then Sporeweb Weaver's ability triggers and is put on the stack the next time a player would receive priority. Nicolas must wait until that trigger actually exists to cast Tishana's Tidebinder — if he casts Tishana's Tidebinder earlier (say, during declare blockers), there is no activated or triggered ability on the stack for its enter-the-battlefield trigger to target, so that trigger simply isn't put on the stack and nothing is countered.

2. This does not save Serpent Assassin. Sporeweb Weaver has deathtouch at the moment combat damage is dealt, so Serpent Assassin is destroyed by state-based actions the instant before any player gets priority — that happens before Nicolas can cast Tishana's Tidebinder. Making Sporeweb Weaver lose deathtouch afterward doesn't undo that.

3. Tishana's Tidebinder can only counter activated or triggered abilities. It can't "counter" reach or deathtouch directly (those are static abilities); it only strips them as a side effect of countering Sporeweb Weaver's damage trigger, and only while Tishana's Tidebinder stays on the battlefield. If Tishana's Tidebinder later leaves the battlefield, Sporeweb Weaver gets its abilities back.

4. Multiplayer makes no difference here: the interaction is entirely between Nicolas's Tishana's Tidebinder and Adrienne's Sporeweb Weaver, and only the trigger's controller (Adrienne) is affected. Other players simply get priority in turn order like normal.

5. If Sporeweb Weaver had somehow died to the combat damage, the trigger would still be on the stack and still counterable by Tishana's Tidebinder, but there would be no permanent left to lose abilities.
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Tishana's Tidebinder's ability targets Sporeweb Weaver's ability, not Sporeweb Weaver itself, so hexproof doesn't matter.

entries.question: Autumn controls [Captain Mar-Vell, Space-Born] and casts [Tempted by the Oriq] targeting Breanna's and Case's Soldier tokens. Before it resolves, Autumn casts [Insurrection]. What happens?
entries.reason: The candidate incorrectly states Tempted by the Oriq's targets remain legal and it resolves, whereas the correct ruling is that its targets (being "creature an opponent controls") become illegal after Insurrection and the spell does not resolve.
entries.answer:
**Short answer: Insurrection resolves first and hands Autumn every creature on the battlefield, including Breanna's and Case's Soldier tokens. When Tempted by the Oriq then resolves, its target(s) are still legal, so it does resolve — but the "gain control" part is redundant (Autumn already controls them) and the untap part does nothing (Insurrection already untapped them). The haste and any pump/keyword bonus Tempted by the Oriq grants still apply.**

How it plays out step by step:

1. **Stack order (last in, first out).** Tempted by the Oriq is put on the stack first, Insurrection goes on top of it. Insurrection is the top object, so Insurrection resolves first while Tempted by the Oriq waits below it (CR 608.1).

2. **Insurrection resolves.** It untaps *all* creatures on the battlefield, Autumn gains control of all of them until end of turn, and they gain haste until end of turn. In a two‑player game that's Autumn's and one opponent's creatures; in a multiplayer game it really is *every* creature every player controls — Breanna's Soldier token, Case's Soldier token, and anyone else's — so the multiplayer answer here is "more creatures," not a different rule.

3. **Tempted by the Oriq resolves.** Tempted by the Oriq is the Strixhaven Act of Treason–style sorcery: gain control of the targeted creature until end of turn, untap it, and it gains haste until end of turn. It does **not** restrict its target to a creature an opponent controls, so the fact that Autumn now controls the Soldier tokens does not make the target illegal. Nothing is countered for having no legal targets (CR 608.2b would only counter it if *all* its targets had become illegal — e.g., if a Soldier token had left the battlefield in response).
   - Gaining control of a permanent you already control simply does nothing observable.
   - Untapping an already‑untapped Soldier token does nothing.
   - Haste is redundant with Insurrection's haste, but any additional bonus Tempted by the Oriq grants still applies normally.

4. **Timestamps.** Both are control‑changing effects (layer 2, CR 613.1b). Tempted by the Oriq's has the later timestamp and therefore "wins," but since both give control to Autumn and both last "until end of turn," there is no practical difference. Both effects end together during the cleanup step (CR 514.2), and the Soldier tokens go back to Breanna and Case — tapped, if Autumn attacked with them, and with any damage still marked until cleanup.

Two practical caveats:

- **Both spells are sorceries.** You normally can't cast Insurrection while Tempted by the Oriq is on the stack. The scenario as described requires Autumn to have flash‑granting help (Vedalken Orrery, Leyline of Anticipation, Teferi, or an ability on Captain Mar-Vell, Space-Born). If Autumn has no such effect, the second cast is simply illegal and gets rewound.
- **Number of targets.** Tempted by the Oriq targets exactly one creature as printed. If Autumn is somehow targeting both Breanna's Soldier token and Case's Soldier token, that must be coming from another effect (an extra‑target or copy effect). I can't verify the printed text of Captain Mar-Vell, Space-Born, so I can't confirm whether it's what's supplying the extra target — but the analysis above applies identically to each target, and if Captain Mar-Vell, Space-Born has a triggered ability keyed to gaining control of creatures or to targeting creatures, that trigger would go on the stack when the relevant event happens and resolve independently of these two spells. Also note that Insurrection's mass control change is not a targeting event, so anything on Captain Mar-Vell, Space-Born that keys off "targets" won't see Insurrection at all.

Also worth knowing for the attack: creatures Autumn gained control of this turn have haste from both spells, so they can attack, and Autumn chooses which opponent (or planeswalker/battle) each one attacks — a Soldier token Autumn stole from Breanna can be sent at Breanna or at Case.
entries.answer_gold: Insurrection resolves and Autumn gains control of all the Soldier tokens. Then Tempted by the Oriq begins to resolve, but its targets are now illegal, so it does not resolve and is removed from the stack.

entries.question: Amelia casts [Aminatou's Augury] exiling an artifact and an instant. Afterwards Amelia casts another Aminatou's Augury, which exiles an instant. Can they cast both instants?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude each Aminatou's Augury creates an independent permission to cast an instant from its own exiled cards, so Amelia can cast both.
entries.answer:
Yes — Amelia can cast both instants, one from each Aminatou's Augury's set of exiled cards.

Why: Aminatou's Augury reads (in essence) "Exile the top eight cards of your library. You may play a land from among them. Until end of turn, for each card type, you may cast a spell of that type from among those cards without paying its mana cost." Each resolution of Aminatou's Augury creates its own, separate continuous effect. That effect only grants permission to cast cards it exiled, and it only tracks spells cast using its own permission. So the first Aminatou's Augury allows one artifact spell, one instant spell, one sorcery spell, etc., from among its eight exiled cards, and the second Aminatou's Augury independently allows one instant (and one of each other type) from among its own eight exiled cards. Casting the instant exiled by the first Aminatou's Augury does not use up the second Aminatou's Augury's instant allowance, and vice versa.

Practical points:
- The artifact from the first Aminatou's Augury is likewise unaffected by any of this; it's a different card type and a different allowance.
- If Amelia cast the second Aminatou's Augury for free using the first Aminatou's Augury's permission, that consumes the first effect's *sorcery* allowance only — the first effect's instant allowance is still available.
- Both permissions last only until end of turn, and the cards stay in exile if unused. Instants can be cast any time Amelia has priority; the second Aminatou's Augury itself, being a sorcery, needed a main phase with an empty stack.
- If a card has multiple types (say, an artifact instant), casting it uses up that effect's allowance for every one of its types.
- I'm assuming the instant exiled by the first Aminatou's Augury hadn't already been cast. If Amelia had already cast an instant off the first Aminatou's Augury, that effect is done granting instants, but the second Aminatou's Augury would still let her cast one instant from its own exiled eight.

Player count doesn't matter here; the answer is the same in a two-player game or a multiplayer game.
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Each Aminatou's Augury creates a separate effect that applies to cards it exiled. Casting an instant off the first Aminatou's Augury doesn't preclude Amelia from casting an instant off the second one.

entries.question: Agustin casts [Seasoned Pyromancer] and has two other cards in hand, one of which is a land card. Nico controls [Leyline of the Void]. How many tokens are created?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion (one token) and correctly explains that Leyline of the Void replaces the cards' destination with exile but does not prevent Seasoned Pyromancer from counting the nonland card as discarded.
entries.answer:
One token.

Seasoned Pyromancer's enters-the-battlefield trigger reads: "When Seasoned Pyromancer enters the battlefield, discard two cards, then draw two cards. For each nonland card discarded this way, create a 1/1 red Elemental creature token." Agustin has exactly two cards in hand at that point (one land, one nonland), so he discards both: one land card and one nonland card. Only the nonland card counts, so Seasoned Pyromancer makes exactly one 1/1 red Elemental token. Agustin then draws two cards.

Leyline of the Void, controlled by Nico, reads "If a card would be put into an opponent's graveyard from anywhere, exile it instead." That's a replacement effect that changes only the *destination* of the discarded cards — assuming Agustin and Nico are opponents, both of Agustin's discarded cards are exiled instead of hitting his graveyard. They are still discarded, though. Discarding means moving a card from its owner's hand to the graveyard, and a replacement effect that redirects it elsewhere doesn't stop the card from having been discarded, so Seasoned Pyromancer still counts the nonland card discarded this way. Leyline of the Void does not reduce the token count.

What Leyline of the Void does change: the discarded cards end up in exile rather than in Agustin's graveyard, so anything that cares about cards in the graveyard (flashback, escape, delirium, Seasoned Pyromancer's own later {3}{R}{R}, exile-from-graveyard activated ability, etc.) can't use them.

Multiplayer note: Leyline of the Void only replaces cards going to an *opponent's* graveyard from Nico's perspective. If this is a multiplayer game and Agustin is Nico's teammate (or otherwise not Nico's opponent), the discarded cards simply go to Agustin's graveyard. Either way, the answer to the question asked is the same — one token.
entries.answer_gold: One token is created. The cards discarded from hand can still be seen by Seasoned Pyromancer's effect even though going to the graveyard was replaced by going to exile.

entries.question: Aranza controls a [Welding Jar] enchanted by Nico's [Curse Artifact]. In response to the trigger during Aranza's upkeep, Nico casts [Word of Seizing] to take control of the Welding Jar. What happens as the trigger resolves?
entries.reason: The candidate says Aranza must pay {1} or lose 1 life and that control change doesn't stop the trigger, whereas the reference says Aranza is dealt 2 damage and cannot sacrifice the Welding Jar she no longer controls, so the conclusions conflict.
entries.answer:
**Aranza is the one who must pay {1} or lose 1 life, even though Nico now controls Welding Jar.** The trigger still resolves normally, and Curse Artifact stays attached to Welding Jar.

Why:

1. **Who the trigger points at is locked in when it triggers.** Curse Artifact's ability triggers "at the beginning of the upkeep of enchanted artifact's controller," and then says *that player* loses 1 life unless they pay {1}. "That player" is a fixed reference to the player identified by the trigger condition at the moment the ability triggered — Aranza, who controlled Welding Jar at the start of her upkeep. Gaining control of Welding Jar afterward with Word of Seizing does not re-point the ability at Nico. On resolution Aranza chooses whether to pay {1} (one generic mana, payable with mana of any color or with colorless mana); if she declines or can't, she loses 1 life.

2. **Nico controls the ability, Aranza makes the payment.** Curse Artifact is Nico's permanent, so Nico controls the triggered ability on the stack. That's irrelevant to who pays — the ability names the player itself rather than saying "you."

3. **Curse Artifact doesn't fall off.** An Aura's controller and the controller of the permanent it enchants don't have to be the same player. Welding Jar changing controllers doesn't make Curse Artifact illegally attached, so it stays on the battlefield attached to Welding Jar (now under Nico's control until end of turn). Word of Seizing also untaps Welding Jar and gives it haste, which matters little for an artifact with no tap abilities.

4. **Split second matters for what Aranza can do.** While Word of Seizing is on the stack, players can't cast spells or activate non-mana abilities. Aranza therefore can't sacrifice Welding Jar to its own regenerate ability in response. Once Word of Seizing has resolved, players get priority again with the Curse Artifact trigger still on the stack — but sacrificing Welding Jar at that point (Nico can now do it, since Nico controls it) would only put Curse Artifact into the graveyard as a state-based action; the trigger already on the stack still resolves, and Aranza still pays {1} or loses 1 life.

Assumed timing: the Curse Artifact trigger was already on the stack when Word of Seizing was cast, exactly as stated. If instead Word of Seizing had resolved *before* Aranza's upkeep began, then Nico would be Welding Jar's controller at the beginning of the upkeep and the ability would trigger on Nico's upkeep instead — meaning it wouldn't trigger during Aranza's upkeep at all that turn.

Multiplayer makes no difference here: the ability only ever concerns the enchanted artifact's controller as of the trigger, so with two players or ten, Aranza is the one on the hook this turn.
entries.answer_gold: Aranza is dealt 2 damage. Sacrificing the Welding Jar is a cost. If the cost isn't paid, the default action of dealing 2 damage to Aranza happens. Aranza cannot sacrifice a permanent that they don't control.

entries.question: Alina controls a [Valakut, the Molten Pinnacle] and 5 [Mountain]s. They plays a 6th Mountain and target Nico with Valakut, the Molten Pinnacle's trigger. In response, Nico activates [Memorial to War], targeting the Valakut, the Molten Pinnacle. Will they be dealt 3 damage?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion as the reference: destroying Valakut after its triggered ability is on the stack doesn't stop the trigger, so it can still resolve and deal 3 damage.
entries.answer:
