Yes — Nico still takes 3 damage (assuming Alina chooses to apply the trigger's "may").

Why destroying Valakut, the Molten Pinnacle doesn't help Nico:

1. An activated or triggered ability on the stack exists independently of its source. Once Valakut, the Molten Pinnacle's triggered ability is on the stack, destroying Valakut, the Molten Pinnacle with Memorial to War does nothing to that ability — it isn't countered and it still resolves. The game uses last known information about Valakut, the Molten Pinnacle (its characteristics as it last existed on the battlefield) to determine the source of the damage.

2. The intervening-"if" clause is rechecked on resolution, and it still holds. Valakut, the Molten Pinnacle reads "Whenever a Mountain enters under your control, if you control at least five other Mountains, you may have Valakut, the Molten Pinnacle deal 3 damage to any target." "Other" means other than the Mountain that just entered. Alina controls six Mountains, so there are five others, and Memorial to War destroyed Valakut, the Molten Pinnacle — which is a legendary land, not a Mountain — so the Mountain count is unchanged. Note that if Memorial to War had instead destroyed one of Alina's Mountains, the condition would fail on resolution (only four other Mountains) and the trigger would do nothing.

3. Nico is still a legal target (nothing in the exchange changed that), so the ability isn't removed from the stack for lack of legal targets.

On resolution Alina decides whether to have the damage dealt (it's a "may"); assuming they say yes, Nico is dealt 3 damage by Valakut, the Molten Pinnacle even though it's now in the graveyard.

Timing assumption: I'm reading the question as the Mountain entering and the trigger going on the stack first, with Memorial to War activated in response. If instead Nico had activated Memorial to War and destroyed Valakut, the Molten Pinnacle before Alina played the sixth Mountain, there would be no permanent on the battlefield to trigger at all, and no damage.

Player count doesn't matter here: the trigger targets "any target," so Alina picked Nico regardless of whether it's a two-player or multiplayer game, and nothing about the interaction changes with more opponents.
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Removing the source of an ability on the stack does not affect that ability.

entries.question: Arely equips [Barbed Batterfist] onto [Champion of the Flame]. Does Champion of the Flame die?
entries.reason: Both the reference and candidate conclude Champion of the Flame does not die — the candidate reaches the same survival ruling despite disagreeing about the final P/T.
entries.answer:
No — Champion of the Flame doesn't die. Attaching Barbed Batterfist to it makes it bigger, not smaller: Champion of the Flame ends up a 6/4 for the turn.

How that breaks down:

- Champion of the Flame is a 2/2 with "Whenever an Aura or Equipment becomes attached to Champion of the Flame, it gets +2/+2 until end of turn."
- Barbed Batterfist is an Artifact — Equipment (with For Mirrodin!, which only matters when it enters the battlefield) whose static ability gives the equipped creature +2/+0. Its equip cost is {2} — two generic mana, payable with mana of any color or with colorless mana.
- Equip is an activated ability that can be activated only any time you could cast a sorcery (your main phase, stack empty, your turn), and it targets a creature you control. When it resolves, Barbed Batterfist becomes attached to Champion of the Flame.
- That attachment immediately triggers Champion of the Flame's ability. With the +2/+0 from Barbed Batterfist applying continuously and the +2/+2 from the trigger once it resolves, Champion of the Flame is 6/4 until end of turn.

Nothing here reduces toughness, so the state-based action that puts a creature with 0 or less toughness into the graveyard never applies, and there's no lethal damage involved. The only ways Champion of the Flame would die in this sequence are unrelated: if it already had 4 or more damage marked on it from earlier in the turn (in which case it would have died before the +2/+2 wore off only if the damage was 4+; with exactly 2 or 3 damage marked it survives while it's a 6/4 and then dies as a state-based action when the +2/+2 ends during the cleanup-step-adjacent moment — practically, at end of turn), or if an opponent responds to the equip ability or the triggered ability with removal. Note that if damage was marked on Champion of the Flame before the pump, that damage stays marked; the pump doesn't remove it.

Player count doesn't matter here — the interaction is identical in a two-player game and in multiplayer, since equip only targets a creature its controller controls.
entries.answer_gold: No, Champion of the Flame will be a 4/2 and not die. All continuous effects are applied instantly before state based actions are checked.

entries.question: Aviana controls a [Meng Huo's Horde] and a [Deathrite Shaman]. Nico controls a [Propaganda]. Can Aviana use Deathrite Shaman's ability to pay for the Meng Huo's Horde to attack?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same final ruling as the reference: Deathrite Shaman’s mana‑producing ability is not a mana ability (because it targets), so it cannot be used to pay Propaganda’s {2} attack tax for Meng Huo’s Horde.
entries.answer:
No. Deathrite Shaman's mana‑producing ability is not a mana ability, so Aviana can't use it to pay Propaganda's {2} attack cost for Meng Huo's Horde.

Why:

1. Deathrite Shaman's first ability is "{T}: Exile target land card from a graveyard. Add one mana of any color." An activated ability is only a mana ability if it could add mana, isn't a loyalty ability, **and doesn't require a target** (CR 605.1a). Because Deathrite Shaman's ability targets a land card in a graveyard, it is a normal activated ability that uses the stack, and it can only be activated when a player has priority.

2. Propaganda says creatures can't attack its controller (Nico) unless their controller pays {2} for each of those creatures — that's {2} generic mana, payable with mana of any color or colorless mana. Paying that cost happens as part of the turn‑based action of declaring attackers in the declare attackers step: attackers are declared, the total attack cost is determined, the active player gets a chance to activate **mana abilities**, and then pays. No player receives priority during that sequence (CR 508.1). Since Deathrite Shaman's ability isn't a mana ability, Aviana has no window to activate it there.

3. Activating Deathrite Shaman earlier doesn't help either: mana pools empty at the end of each step and phase (CR 500.4). Mana made during Aviana's precombat main phase or during the beginning of combat step is gone before attackers are declared. Aviana needs mana available at the moment attackers are declared — from lands or from true mana abilities (ones that don't target), which she can activate during the declare‑attackers turn‑based action.

Also note Deathrite Shaman's other two abilities ({B}, {T} exile an instant/sorcery card; {G}, {T} exile a creature card) don't produce mana at all, so they're irrelevant here.

On Meng Huo's Horde specifically: if Meng Huo's Horde has an additional "can't attack unless you pay" cost of its own, that cost is determined and paid at the same moment as Propaganda's {2}, and the same conclusion applies — Deathrite Shaman can't pay for it.

Multiplayer note: Propaganda only taxes attacks against Nico. If there are other players (or planeswalkers controlled by other players) and Aviana declares Meng Huo's Horde as attacking someone other than Nico, no {2} is owed at all and the question is moot. With exactly two players, Nico is always the defending player, so the tax always applies.
entries.answer_gold: No. Propaganda imposes a cost on Meng Huo's Horde attacking, which must be paid as a part of declaring it as an attacker. Deathrite Shaman's ability is not a mana ability, so the last time it could be activated before attackers are declared is during the beginning of combat step. At the end of that step, the mana would empty from Aviana's mana pool.

entries.question: Amos casts [Rise from the Grave] targeting [Rhizome Lurcher] in their graveyard. Assuming there are no other cards in any graveyards, how many +1/+1 counters will Rhizome Lurcher enter the battlefield with?
entries.reason: The candidate concludes Rhizome Lurcher enters with zero counters, contradicting the correct ruling that the replacement effect counts the card types in Amos's graveyard as it enters and thus counts itself for one counter.
entries.answer:
**Zero.** Rhizome Lurcher enters the battlefield with no +1/+1 counters, so it's a 0/0 and is put into Amos's graveyard immediately as a state-based action.

Why:

- Rhizome Lurcher is a 0/0 creature that enters the battlefield with a +1/+1 counter on it for each *card type* among cards in your graveyard ("your" = the controller of Rhizome Lurcher, i.e., Amos). This is a replacement effect, so the count is made as Rhizome Lurcher enters the battlefield, using the game state at that exact moment.
- At that moment, Rhizome Lurcher has already left the graveyard — it's the object being put onto the battlefield, so it can't count itself.
- Rise from the Grave is still on the stack while it's resolving. An instant or sorcery spell is only put into its owner's graveyard as the *final* part of its resolution, which happens after Rhizome Lurcher has already entered the battlefield. So Rise from the Grave doesn't contribute its sorcery type to the count either.
- With the stipulation that there are no other cards in any graveyard, Amos's graveyard has zero card types among it, giving zero counters. Rhizome Lurcher enters as a 0/0 black Zombie (Rise from the Grave makes it a black Zombie in addition to its other types) and dies the next time state-based actions are checked, since a creature with 0 or less toughness is put into its owner's graveyard.

A couple of clarifications:

- Rhizome Lurcher counts card *types* (artifact, creature, enchantment, instant, land, planeswalker, sorcery, battle, etc.), not the number of cards, and it only looks at Amos's graveyard — cards in opponents' graveyards never matter, so the answer is the same in a two-player or multiplayer game.
- If instead you're picturing that Rise from the Grave had already finished resolving and hit the graveyard before Rhizome Lurcher entered, that's not how resolution works, but note that even then the second Zombie-making clause and the counter count are locked in as it enters — the timing is fixed: Rhizome Lurcher enters first, Rise from the Grave goes to the graveyard second.
- Practically, to get any counters you'd want other card types already sitting in Amos's graveyard before Rise from the Grave resolves.
entries.answer_gold: One. Rhizome Lurcher has a replacement effect that modifies how it will enter the battlefield. The game needs to know how Rhizome Lurcher will enter the battlefield, and must do that before it enters the battlefield. At that point it will be in the graveyard and will count itself.

entries.question: Ava controls [Undead Minotaur] enchanted with [Shade's Form]. Nico casts [Hour of Revelation] to destroy both Undead Minotaur and Shade's Form. Will Undead Minotaur return to the battlefield?
entries.reason: The candidate agrees Shade's Form's triggered ability returns Undead Minotaur to the battlefield (adding that it then likely dies as a 0/0), which matches the reference's core ruling that it does return.
entries.answer:
Yes — Shade's Form's ability still triggers and Undead Minotaur does come back — but it returns as a 0/0 and is immediately put back into the graveyard by state-based actions.

Why the trigger works even though Shade's Form died too:

- Hour of Revelation destroys all nonland permanents simultaneously, so Undead Minotaur and Shade's Form are put into the graveyard at the same time.
- Shade's Form's ability is a "leaves-the-battlefield" style trigger ("When enchanted creature dies..."). These abilities look back in time at the game state immediately before the event, so the ability sees that Shade's Form was on the battlefield attached to Undead Minotaur when Undead Minotaur died. It triggers even though Shade's Form itself was destroyed by the same spell (CR 603.6e/603.10).
- The trigger is put on the stack after Hour of Revelation finishes resolving, and Ava's opponents get priority before it resolves.

What happens when the trigger resolves:

- Undead Minotaur returns from the graveyard to the battlefield as a brand-new object (CR 400.7). Shade's Form does not return; it stays in the graveyard.
- The returning effect makes Undead Minotaur a black Shade with base power and toughness 0/0 (applied in layer 7b) and grants it "{B}: This creature gets +1/+1 until end of turn."
- State-based actions are checked before any player receives priority, and a creature with toughness 0 or less is put into its owner's graveyard (CR 704.5a). So Undead Minotaur hits the battlefield and dies again immediately. Ava gets no window to activate the {B} pump ability first.
- Practical exception: if some continuous effect already on the battlefield boosts it (an anthem effect from a land, an emblem, etc.), Undead Minotaur would survive as, e.g., a 1/1 Shade. Right after Hour of Revelation that's unlikely, since all nonland permanents were destroyed.
- Note the second death is a new dies event, but Shade's Form is no longer attached to anything, so nothing triggers again.

Timing caveat: I'm assuming Shade's Form was attached to Undead Minotaur at the moment Hour of Revelation resolved. If Shade's Form had already left the battlefield before Hour of Revelation resolved (for example, it was destroyed by an earlier spell and Undead Minotaur died later), there would be no trigger at all and Undead Minotaur would simply stay in the graveyard.

Player count makes no difference: Hour of Revelation hits all nonland permanents regardless of controller, and Shade's Form's trigger works identically in a two-player or multiplayer game.
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Shade's Form has a triggered ability that occurs when the enchanted permanent dies. For most triggers the game checks to see if they occur right after every event. However for "dies" triggers the game checks what the game state looked like right before they triggered to see if they trigger. In this case, checking right before Hour of Revelation resolved results in Shade's Form triggering and returning Undead Minotaur to the battlefield.

entries.question: Amara controls [Muraganda Petroglyphs] and [Wayward Angel], and has more than 7 cards in their graveyard. Nehemiah casts and resolves [Humility]. What are Wayward Angel's characteristics?
entries.reason: The candidate wrongly concludes the threshold +3/+3 is lost when Humility strips abilities (yielding 3/3), but the correct ruling is the P/T effect from the threshold still applies, making Wayward Angel a 6/6 with no abilities.
entries.answer:
**Wayward Angel ends up as a 3/3 black Creature — Angel named Wayward Angel with mana cost {4}{W}{W} and no abilities at all** (no flying, no threshold ability, no granted regeneration ability).

How that shakes out, layer by layer (CR 613 applies continuous effects in a fixed order, not in timestamp order across layers):

- **Layer 5 (color).** Wayward Angel's threshold ability ("as long as seven or more cards are in your graveyard, Wayward Angel gets +3/+3, is black, and has 'Sacrifice a creature: Regenerate Wayward Angel'") still exists when layer 5 is applied, because ability removal doesn't happen until layer 6. Amara has more than seven cards in the graveyard, so Wayward Angel is **black** here rather than white.
- **Layer 6 (abilities).** Two effects want to apply: Wayward Angel's own threshold ability granting "Sacrifice a creature: Regenerate Wayward Angel," and Humility removing all abilities from all creatures. These are ordered by timestamp; Humility resolved most recently, so first Wayward Angel gains the regeneration ability, then Humility strips everything — flying, the threshold ability itself, and the granted regeneration ability. After layer 6, Wayward Angel has **no abilities**.
- **Layer 7b (setting P/T).** Humility sets Wayward Angel's base power and toughness to **1/1**.
- **Layer 7c (P/T modifications).** The threshold ability no longer exists (it was removed back in layer 6), so its +3/+3 never applies. Muraganda Petroglyphs, however, is a separate permanent whose ability was not removed (Muraganda Petroglyphs is an enchantment, and Humility only affects creatures). Muraganda Petroglyphs checks whether the creature has no abilities *at the time layer 7c is applied* — Wayward Angel now has none, so it gets **+2/+2**.

1/1 base, +2/+2 = **3/3**.

A couple of notes:

- The "is black" part surviving while the "+3/+3" part doesn't is the intended, if counterintuitive, result of the layer order: parts of a single ability's effect apply in their own layers, and only the parts in layers *after* layer 6 are lost when Humility strips the ability. If you're playing with a Wayward Angel printing whose threshold clause doesn't include a color change, then Wayward Angel simply stays white; everything else is the same.
- Muraganda Petroglyphs affects **every** creature with no abilities, not just Amara's, so all creatures on the battlefield (which Humility has made ability-less 1/1s) will likewise be 3/3s — unless something gives one of them an ability with a timestamp later than Humility's, in which case that creature loses the Muraganda Petroglyphs bonus and is a 1/1.
- Nothing here changes with more than two players; Humility and Muraganda Petroglyphs both apply globally to all creatures regardless of controller or player count.
entries.answer_gold:
Wayward Angel is a Black, 6/6 creature with no abilities. The rest of its characteristics remain the same as printed on the card. 
Wayward Angel's threshold ability changes both its color, abilities, and P/T. Therefore, it applies in layers 5, 6, and 7 with the appropriate parts applying in their appropriate layers, and the layers are applied in order. Similarly, Humility's effect is applied in layers 6 and 7, as appropriate. 
Applying layers in order:
- In layer 5, Wayward Angel becomes black. 
- In layer 6 there are two contending effects: Wayward Angel's ability giving it trample and an upkeep triggered ability, and Humility's ability removing all abilities from Wayward Angel. There is no dependency between the two, since Wayward Angel's ability has already started applying in a previous layer, and will continue to apply even if removed by Humility's ability. The effects are then applied in timestamp order with Wayward Angel's ability applying first, since it has an earlier timestamp. So in layer 6, Wayward Angel first gains trample and "At the beginning of your upkeep, sacrifice a creature.", and then loses all abilities to Humility.
- In layer 7, P/T setting effects are applied first, so that Humility first turns Wayward Angel into a 1/1. Then effects modifying P/T are applied, of which there are two: Wayward Angel's own ability that, even though removed, continues to apply and gives it +3/+3, and Muraganda Petroglyphs's ability giving Wayward Angel +2/+2 since it now has no abilities. Wayward Angel's P/T is finally 6/6.

entries.question: Nayeli controls [Trinisphere]. Ainsley casts [Noxious Revival], paying 2 life for the Phyrexian mana. What is the total cost of the Noxious Revival?
entries.reason: The candidate says Ainsley pays two mana and 2 life, but the correct ruling is that Trinisphere raises the spell’s mana cost to three, so the total payment is three mana plus 2 life.
entries.answer:
Noxious Revival's total cost becomes {2}{G/P} — three mana total — and Ainsley pays {2} in generic mana plus 2 life (the life payment satisfies the {G/P} symbol, but it does not count as "mana paid" for Trinisphere's purposes).

Why:

- Noxious Revival's mana cost is {G/P}, a Phyrexian green mana symbol. A Phyrexian mana symbol can be paid either with one mana of that color ({G} here) or by paying 2 life. Either way, the symbol is still one mana symbol in the spell's cost.
- Trinisphere reads that as long as it's untapped, if a spell would cost less than three mana to cast, that spell instead costs an amount of generic mana that brings its total cost to three mana. When Ainsley announces Noxious Revival, the cost is calculated in step 601.2f, after any cost reductions and with cost increases such as Trinisphere's applied last.
- For that calculation, the {G/P} symbol counts as one mana, regardless of whether Ainsley intends to pay life for it. So Noxious Revival would cost only one mana, and Trinisphere adds {2} to bring the total to three mana: {2}{G/P}.
- In the payment step, Ainsley pays the {2} with any two mana (any colors and/or colorless) and then chooses to pay 2 life for the {G/P}. Paying life does not reduce the {2}; the added generic mana must be paid with actual mana. Total outlay: two mana and 2 life.

A couple of notes:

- If Trinisphere is tapped when Noxious Revival is cast, it has no effect at all, and Noxious Revival costs just {G/P} — payable entirely with 2 life and no mana.
- Trinisphere affects spells cast by every player, including Nayeli's own, and this works the same whether the game has two players or more; nothing here depends on player count.
- If any cost reduction applied to Noxious Revival, it would still be floored at three total mana by Trinisphere as long as Trinisphere is untapped when the cost is locked in during casting. Once the total cost is determined, Trinisphere later becoming tapped or leaving the battlefield doesn't change the cost Ainsley must pay.
entries.answer_gold: {3} and 2 life. While casting Noxious Revival, Ainsley chooses whether to pay life or mana for each Phyrexian mana symbol in the cost. Trinisphere is applied afterwards and increases the cost up to the minimum of 3 mana.

entries.question: Anakin controls [Mycosynth Lattice], an [Animate Dead] attached to a [Maritime Guard] that it returned to the battlefield, and a [Mizzium Transreliquat] that is currently a copy of [Sakashima of a Thousand Faces] due to its second ability. Anakin casts [Clever Impersonator], choosing to copy the Mizzium Transreliquat and then choosing to copy the Animate Dead with its new copy ability as it enters the battlefield. They choose to enchant a [Balduvian Barbarians] in their graveyard. After Clever Impersonator's trigger resolves and returns the Balduvian Barbarians to the battlefield, Anakin activates the ability of the Clever Impersonator to turn it into a copy of Maritime Guard. What happens?
entries.reason: The reference says the described copy of Animate Dead via Sakashima is illegal and the scenario can't happen, while the candidate accepts that copy and gives a different end state where Clever Impersonator becomes Maritime Guard and detaches.
entries.answer:
**Short version of the end state:** Clever Impersonator stops being a copy of Animate Dead and becomes a copy of Maritime Guard (a 1/3 Merfolk Soldier named Maritime Guard) that additionally has "{3}{U}{R}: This permanent becomes a copy of target artifact, except it has this ability. Activate only as a sorcery." Because it is no longer an Aura, a state-based action immediately unattaches it from Balduvian Barbarians. Balduvian Barbarians stays on the battlefield and reverts to a 3/3, since the current Oracle text of Animate Dead has no "destroy/sacrifice the creature when this leaves" clause and the -1/-0 came from an ability the permanent no longer has.

**Why each piece works:**

- **Targeting Maritime Guard is legal.** Mycosynth Lattice says every permanent is an artifact in addition to its other types, so Maritime Guard is an artifact creature and a legal "target artifact" for the Mizzium Transreliquat ability. Mycosynth Lattice also lets Anakin spend mana as though it were mana of any color, so any five mana pays {3}{U}{R} — but note {C} (colorless mana) is not "mana of any color," so colorless mana can only pay the {3} generic portion.
- **Clever Impersonator has that ability at all** because copy effects use copiable values: Mizzium Transreliquat's copiable values were "Sakashima of a Thousand Faces, except it has the {3}{U}{R} ability," so copying Mizzium Transreliquat gave Clever Impersonator that whole package.
- **The new copy effect overwrites the old one.** Both copy effects apply in layer 1 in timestamp order, and the newest one says "becomes a copy of Maritime Guard, except it has this ability." So the Animate Dead text (the Aura subtype, "Enchanted creature gets -1/-0," the enter-the-battlefield trigger) and the Sakashima of a Thousand Faces name/legendary exceptions are all gone. The permanent is now named Maritime Guard, isn't legendary, and is an artifact creature via Mycosynth Lattice, colorless via Mycosynth Lattice.
- **Unattaching:** a permanent that is neither an Aura, Equipment, nor Fortification cannot stay attached, so it simply becomes unattached and remains on the battlefield. The leftover continuous effect from the Animate Dead trigger ("gains 'enchant creature put onto the battlefield with Animate Dead'") still technically applies, but an enchant ability does nothing on a permanent that isn't an Aura, so it doesn't keep it attached.
- **Balduvian Barbarians is safe.** Animate Dead's return-to-the-battlefield is a one-shot effect from its trigger. Nothing in the Oracle text kills the creature if the Aura stops enchanting it (that's Necromancy/Dance of the Dead behavior, not Animate Dead's current Oracle text).
- **Summoning sickness:** the new Maritime Guard copy came under Anakin's control this turn, so it can't attack or use {T} abilities this turn. The Mizzium Transreliquat ability has no {T} in its cost, so it was fine to activate (assuming a main phase with an empty stack, since it's sorcery-speed only).
- Note the original Maritime Guard, still enchanted by the original Animate Dead, is a 0/3; the new copy is a 1/3, because the -1/-0 from the original Animate Dead isn't a copiable value.

**One legality flag on an earlier step:** Sakashima of a Thousand Faces' enters-the-battlefield ability reads "as a copy of any *creature* on the battlefield." Mycosynth Lattice makes Animate Dead an artifact, not a creature, so strictly speaking Clever Impersonator couldn't use that ability to copy Animate Dead. If you play it strictly, Clever Impersonator would just have entered as Mizzium Transreliquat's copiable values (a Sakashima of a Thousand Faces with the {3}{U}{R} ability), Balduvian Barbarians would never have come back, and the later activation would simply turn it into the Maritime Guard copy described above with no Aura or detachment involved. The answer above assumes the scenario as written (that the copy of Animate Dead was made and resolved).

**Multiplayer:** nothing here depends on the number of players — every permanent involved is Anakin's, and no ability says "each opponent" or requires choosing a defending player. The answer is identical in two-player and multiplayer games.
entries.answer_gold: This can't happen as described. When Clever Impersonator enters the battlefield and copies Sakashima of a Thousand Faces, it then hard Sakashima of a Thousand Faces's ability to enter the battlefield as a copy of a creature, but it's attempting to copy an enchantment. This is illegal, since Sakashima of a Thousand Faces can only copy creatures, not enchantments.

entries.question: Amare casts [Insatiable Hemophage] targeting [Canal Monitor] to mutate unto it. Can Nico cast [Withering Boon] to counter Insatiable Hemophage?
entries.reason: Both say a spell cast for its mutate cost is still a creature spell on the stack and thus can be targeted and countered by Withering Boon.
entries.answer:
Yes. A spell cast for its mutate cost is still a creature spell while it's on the stack, so Withering Boon — an instant that says "Counter target creature spell" (with the additional cost of paying 1 life) — can legally target and counter Insatiable Hemophage.

Details:

- Mutate is a keyword alternative cost that lets you cast the creature spell targeting a non-Human creature you own (here, Canal Monitor). The spell doesn't become an Aura or anything else; it remains a creature spell with all its normal characteristics until it resolves and merges with Canal Monitor. That's exactly what Withering Boon is allowed to counter.
- Amare casting Insatiable Hemophage for its mutate cost uses the stack normally, so Nico gets priority with Insatiable Hemophage on the stack and can cast Withering Boon (paying {1}{B} plus 1 life) then.
- If Withering Boon resolves, Insatiable Hemophage is countered and put into Amare's graveyard. Canal Monitor is completely unaffected — it stays on the battlefield as its normal self, and Insatiable Hemophage's mutate trigger (the "whenever this creature mutates" life-loss/life-gain ability) never triggers, because no mutation ever happened.
- Alternative line for Nico: instead of countering, Nico could remove or otherwise make Canal Monitor an illegal target in response (kill it, exile it, give it protection, etc.). If the mutate target is illegal on resolution, Insatiable Hemophage doesn't resolve at all — it's put into the graveyard rather than entering the battlefield as an ordinary creature.
- Multiplayer note: none of this changes with more than two players. Withering Boon can counter a creature spell cast by any opponent, and Insatiable Hemophage's mutate trigger (which would have drained each opponent) simply never occurs. The only difference is that its trigger would have hit every opponent, not just Nico.
entries.answer_gold: Yes, Nico can use Withering Boon to counter Insatiable Hemophage if it was cast for the mutate cost. A spell that was cast for a mutate cost is still a creature spell and, therefore, can be countered by Withering Boon. ([702.140a])

entries.question: Amirah controls Azors Gateway with 4 different CMC cards exiled by it. They targets it with [Karn's Touch]. After that resolves, they activates [Azor's Gateway], and transforms it into [Sanctum of the Sun]. What are the characteristics of the new object after it has transformed?
entries.reason: The candidate concludes the permanent is no longer a land (Karn's Touch replaces card types), but the reference states the continuous effect persists and the object is a legendary 2/2 artifact creature land, so the final rulings conflict.
entries.answer:
**Direct answer:** The permanent is now a legendary, colorless **artifact creature named Sanctum of the Sun** with power and toughness 2/2, whose only ability is "{T}: Add X mana of any one color, where X is your life total." It is untapped, has no mana cost (mana value 2), and — because Karn's Touch sets its card types rather than adding to them — it is **not a land** for the rest of the turn.

**Why:**

1. **Karn's Touch keeps applying after the transform.** Transforming doesn't create a new object and doesn't move the permanent between zones; it just changes which face is up, which changes the permanent's copiable characteristics. A continuous effect from a resolved spell locks in the set of objects it affects when it resolves (CR 611.2c), so Karn's Touch's effect keeps applying to that same permanent even though the permanent is no longer a "noncreature artifact" (target legality is only checked on announcement and resolution).

2. **Layer order.** The transform sets the object's base characteristics to those of the Sanctum of the Sun face (Legendary Land, no mana cost, the mana ability). Karn's Touch then applies in layer 4 on top of that, and in layer 7b for power/toughness.

3. **Types.** Karn's Touch says the permanent "becomes an artifact creature." An effect that changes an object's card types replaces the existing card types unless it says "in addition to its other types" or "it's still a land" (compare Blinkmoth Nexus or Celestial Colonnade, which explicitly say they're still lands). So Sanctum of the Sun's Land type is replaced: it's an Artifact Creature with no creature subtypes. The supertype Legendary is unaffected (supertypes aren't removed by a card‑type change), and Sanctum of the Sun is legendary anyway.

4. **Power/toughness.** Karn's Touch sets P/T equal to the object's mana value. The back face of a transforming double-faced card has no mana cost, but its mana value is that of the front face — Azor's Gateway costs {2} — so the mana value is 2 and Sanctum of the Sun is 2/2. (This value is recalculated continuously, but nothing here changes it.)

5. **Abilities.** Type-changing effects don't remove or add abilities. It loses Azor's Gateway's "{1}, {T}: Draw a card…" ability simply because that ability belongs to the other face, and it has Sanctum of the Sun's mana ability. That mana ability still works fine even though the permanent isn't a land.

6. **Status / summoning sickness.** The transform ability untaps it, so it's untapped. Since Amirah had to pay {T} to activate Azor's Gateway while it was already a creature, it must have been under their control since the turn began (or have haste), so it isn't summoning sick — it can attack or tap again if given the chance.

**Practical consequences this turn:** it can be targeted by removal that hits creatures, it dies to 2 damage or −2/−2, and effects that count "lands you control" won't see it. When Karn's Touch's "until end of turn" effect expires during the cleanup step, it reverts to being just a Legendary Land named Sanctum of the Sun.

**Assumption on the transform itself:** you said 4 different mana values were exiled before activating. Azor's Gateway's ability first draws a card and exiles a card from hand, so the transform only happens if that newly exiled card brought the count to five or more different mana values and Amirah paid the extra {5}; I've assumed that happened. If the fifth distinct mana value wasn't achieved, nothing transforms and you simply have an animated 2/2 Azor's Gateway.

**Player count:** none of this changes between a two-player and a multiplayer game.

**If you play it the other way:** some players read "becomes an artifact creature" as additive. It isn't — the only difference under that (incorrect) reading would be that the permanent would also still be a Land.
entries.answer_gold: Sanctum of the Sun is a 2/2 Legendary artifact creature land with the ability "{T}: Add X mana of any one color, where X is your life total". The requirement that Azor's Gateway be an artifact is part of the targeting restriction of the spell, after the spell resolves, it creates a continuous effect on the permanent that was targeted (in this case Azor's Gateway) that lasts until end of turn. When a double-faced card transforms it doesn't become a new object, and any effects that applied to it before the transformation will continue to apply afterwards.

entries.question: Aryana controls [Ascended Lawmage] and [Cemetery Gate]. Nicholas controls [Onakke Ogre] enchanted by their [Paralyze]. Aryana casts [Sudden Disappearance] targeting Nicholas. When the trigger resolves at the beginning of the next end step, what can Paralyze enchant?
entries.reason: The candidate wrongly allows Paralyze to reattach to Onakke Ogre — the reference says only Ascended Lawmage is legal because the Aura's attachment is chosen as the objects return and Onakke Ogre isn't a valid choice at that time.
entries.answer:
**Direct answer: Nicholas chooses, and Paralyze can enchant either Onakke Ogre (which returns from exile at the same moment) or Aryana's Ascended Lawmage. It cannot enchant Cemetery Gate, because Cemetery Gate has protection from black and Paralyze is a black Aura.**

Why:

1. **What Sudden Disappearance did.** Sudden Disappearance exiles all nontoken permanents Nicholas controls — that includes both Onakke Ogre and Paralyze — and creates a delayed trigger that returns those cards to the battlefield under their owners' control at the beginning of the next end step. While in exile they are new, memoryless objects, so Paralyze does not "remember" that it was attached to Onakke Ogre; the attachment is gone.

2. **Who picks, and when.** Paralyze is entering the battlefield without being cast, and the effect doesn't say what it enchants, so the player it's entering under (Nicholas, as its owner) chooses a legal creature for it to enchant as it enters (CR 303.4f). This choice is not targeting — no spell or ability is targeting anything here.

3. **Onakke Ogre is a legal choice.** Everything returns simultaneously in one event, and an Aura returning this way may be attached to a permanent that entered the battlefield at the same time. So Nicholas may re-attach Paralyze to Onakke Ogre. If he does, Paralyze's own "When Paralyze enters the battlefield, tap enchanted creature" trigger goes on the stack and taps Onakke Ogre (permanents return untapped otherwise), and Onakke Ogre won't untap during Nicholas's untap step.

4. **Ascended Lawmage is a legal choice despite hexproof.** Hexproof (and shroud, if you're using the older printed wording of Ascended Lawmage) only stops the permanent from being the *target* of spells and abilities. Attaching an Aura as it enters the battlefield from exile involves no targeting, so nothing stops Nicholas from choosing Ascended Lawmage, even though Aryana controls it. Nicholas would then tap Ascended Lawmage with Paralyze's ETB trigger and keep it from untapping.

5. **Cemetery Gate is not a legal choice.** Protection from black means, among other things, that Cemetery Gate can't be enchanted by black Auras. Paralyze is black, so choosing Cemetery Gate is illegal regardless of targeting (CR 702.16, protection; CR 702.11, hexproof).

Edge cases: If for some reason no legal creature existed for Paralyze to enchant, Paralyze would simply stay in exile rather than entering the battlefield (CR 303.4g); it would not go to the graveyard, since it isn't on the stack. In a multiplayer game, Nicholas may also choose any other player's creature that Paralyze can legally enchant — the rule is the same, since no targeting is involved; the only creatures off-limits are ones with protection from black (or from enchantments/from Nicholas, etc.). Nothing about Sudden Disappearance's split second matters at this point — split second only restricted responses while Sudden Disappearance was on the stack.
entries.answer_gold: Just Ascended Lawmage. Cemetery Gate has protection from black, so it can't be enchanted by anything black. Onakke Ogre isn't on the battlefield when Nicholas chooses what to enchant. Hexproof doesn't prevent an Aura from becoming attached to the Ascended Lawmage.

entries.question: Amaris controls [Eruth, Tormented Prophet] and, during their draw step, they attempt to dredge [Golgari Grave-Troll]. What happens?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Amaris (the affected player) chooses which replacement effect applies (dredge or Eruth's exile) and once one replaces the draw the other no longer applies.
entries.answer:
Amaris gets to choose, and if they choose dredge, the dredge works normally: the draw is replaced by putting the top six cards of Amaris's library into their graveyard and returning Golgari Grave-Troll from the graveyard to their hand. Eruth, Tormented Prophet's replacement effect does nothing for that draw, because there is no longer a draw for it to replace.

Why: both Eruth, Tormented Prophet ("If you would draw a card, instead exile the top two cards of your library...") and dredge ("If you would draw a card, you may instead mill N cards and return this card from your graveyard to your hand") are replacement effects that apply to the same event — Amaris drawing a card during their draw step. When two or more replacement effects would apply to the same event, the affected player (here Amaris, the player who would draw) chooses which one to apply. Each of these effects completely replaces the draw, so once one is applied the other has nothing left to modify:

- Apply dredge: mill 6, return Golgari Grave-Troll to hand, no card is drawn, and Eruth, Tormented Prophet never exiles anything for that draw.
- Apply Eruth, Tormented Prophet instead: exile the top two cards, and Amaris may play them this turn; the draw is gone, so Golgari Grave-Troll can't be dredged off that same draw.

Important practical caveats:

1. Dredge is only a legal choice if Amaris's library has at least six cards (dredge 6 on Golgari Grave-Troll). With five or fewer, dredge simply can't be applied and Eruth, Tormented Prophet's effect is the only one available.
2. Eruth, Tormented Prophet also says "You can't cast spells from your hand." So the Golgari Grave-Troll that returns to Amaris's hand can't be cast while Eruth, Tormented Prophet's effect applies — Amaris would need to dredge it again off a later draw, or get it out another way. Dredging is still fine for filling the graveyard (and Golgari Grave-Troll's power depends on creature cards in your graveyard), it just doesn't give Amaris a castable card.
3. The choice is made each time a draw would happen, so on a draw with multiple replacement options Amaris re-chooses each time.

This is the same in a two-player game and in multiplayer — the choice belongs to the player who would draw, and no opponent gets input.
entries.answer_gold: Amaris can dredge Golgari Grave-Troll instead of drawing. There are two replacement effects attempting to replace Amaris's draw. Since they are the affected player, they choose whether to exile the card with Eruth, Tormented Prophet or dredge with Golgari Grave-Troll. Once one of the replacement effects has been applied, the "draw" event no longer exists, and the other replacement effect does not apply.
